1. Introduction

Eastern boundary currents are typically associated with upwelling of nutrient-replete water into the euphotic zone, high primary productivity on the continental shelf and rich coastal fisheries (Codispoti, 1983). The oceanographic conditions off the coast of Western Australia (WA) however, are dominated by the Leeuwin Current (LC), which suppresses upwelling, transports nutrient-poor water along the continental shelf and has a negative impact on primary productivity (Hanson et al., 2005b; Pearce, 1991). Consequently, the biological oceanography of the WA coast is unique amongst all other west facing coastlines. The absence of large-scale upwelling, in the presence of upwelling favourable southerly winds, ensures that the coastal waters are oligotrophic and that phytoplankton biomass and primary productivity are low in comparison with upwelling zones. For example, upwelling associated with the Humboldt Current off the west coast of Chile delivers

</page>

<page number="1">

nutrient-rich water to the euphotic zone, which in turn supports high primary productivity and efficient trophic transfer of nutrients to a rich pelagic fishery (Alheit and Bernal, 1993). In contrast, the pelagic fishery off the coast of south-west WA is limited by low primary productivity and commercial fishing is dominated by the benthic rock lobster industry, which is Australia’s largest single species industry (Caputi et al., 2001; Gaughan et al., 2001).

Hanson et al. (2005a, b) showed that waters associated with the LC off the coast of WA were largely devoid of dissolved nitrogen (N). In oligotrophic coastal regions the availability of nutrients, in particular N, dictates the magnitude and spatial extent of phytoplankton productivity (Howarth, 1988). Where the input of new nutrients are limited, phytoplankton productivity is maintained by in situ nutrient regeneration (Howarth, 1988), or where N-fixing organisms are present, through atmospheric N acquisition (Paerl et al., 1981). N-fixing phytoplankton are favoured in tropical and subtropical oligotrophic waters, where N\(_2\) may supply more than 50% of the N demand, which can be equivalent to 50–180% of NO\(_3^-\) supplied from depth (Arrigo, 2005; Capone et al., 2005). In light of these estimates, there is great potential for N-fixing phytoplankton to dominate the community composition in WA waters, where they may supply a large proportion of new N to the euphotic zone.

However, the Capes Current which flows in an equatorial direction and extends in-shore of the LC in the south-west of WA (Pearce and Pattiaratchi, 1999) has been shown to promote upwelling during summer when prevailing wind conditions are favourable (Gersbach et al., 1999; Hanson et al., 2005a, b). Upwelling events extending across the continental shelf width are predicted to occur 5–9 times during the summer (Gersbach et al., 1999), which stimulates phytoplankton productivity. Capes Current waters have significantly higher primary productivity compared to those of the LC (Hanson et al., 2005b). The comparatively higher rates of primary productivity in the Capes Current are largely fuelled by the injection of deep water nitrate into the euphotic zone during short-lived upwelling events (Hanson et al., 2005a, b).

This paper investigates N dynamics associated with phytoplankton communities off the south-west coast of WA. The research was designed to investigate N uptake along the shelf, shelf-break and offshore Indian Ocean waters to determine the relative preference for water-column regenerated N versus upwelled new N, and the relative contribution of N fixation.

2. Methods

The present study was conducted aboard the Australian National Facility R.V. Southern Surveyor (SS09/03) from 24 October to 9 November 2003. The study site was located between the Abrolhos Islands and Cape Leeuwin (ca. 28°S and 36°S) adjacent to the coastline of south-west WA (Fig. 1). Fourteen cross-shelf transects were sampled (A–N) with 10–15 stations on each transect

depending on the continental shelf width (total stations = 212). The stations were categorised depending on bottom depth to encompass continental shelf (0–200 m), shelf break (200–300 m) and offshore (300–2000 m) waters. A shipborne acoustic Doppler current profiler (ADCP) enabled measurement of the vertical structure of the currents in 8 m bins to a maximum depth of approximately 300 m.

Hydrographic parameters were collected using a Seabird SBE911 conductivity–temperature–depth (CTD) profiler, fitted with a Seabird SBE32, 24-Niskin bottle rosette sampler. The CTD was equipped with a Licor LI-192SA PAR sensor and a Chelsea Aqua Tracka Fluorometre. Depending on bottom depth, water was collected from between 3 and 15 discrete depths. Dissolved inorganic nutrients (nitrate/nitrite, phosphate and silicate) were analysed onboard with a Lachat Autoanalyser with detections limits of 0.016, 0.01 and 0.15 μM, respectively. Chlorophyll (Chl) \( a \) extraction was performed on 2-L samples filtered onto 25-mm Whatman GF/F filters. Pigments were extracted immediately in 90% acetone following the acidification technique described by Parsons et al. (1984), and read on a Turner Designs TD700 lab fluorometre according to the acidification method of Parsons et al. (1984). For comparative statistics the chlorophyll \( a \) data were transformed (natural log) to satisfy statistical tests of normality and homogeneity of variance. Water samples for ammonium analysis were immediately frozen and stored in the dark until they were returned to the CSIRO Floreat Marine Laboratories. Ammonium analyses were executed on a Lachat autoanalyser using the technique of Kerouel and Aminot (1997) adapted for flow injection by Watson et al. (2004), detect limit \( \sim 0.016 \) μM.

Uptake rates of \( ^{15}\mathrm{N} \) labelled \( \mathrm{NO}_3^- \) and \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) were measured in whole water samples collected from the surface and deep chlorophyll maximum (DCM) depth. Duplicate 500-mL samples were added to acid-washed Nalgene\textregistered{} PET media bottles and incubated within an on-deck incubator with temperature regulation provided by continuous surface seawater flow. Light attenuation for the DCM samples (1% of surface irradiance) was achieved using neutral density screens. The nitrate and ammonium concentrations were unknown at the time of incubation. Therefore experiments were initiated by adding estimated trace amounts (0.05 μM) of \( \mathrm{K}^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^- \) and \( ^{15}\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl} \). Incubations were terminated after 4–6 h of incubation by filtration onto pre-combusted (500 \( ^\circ \mathrm{C} \), 12 h) 25-mm Whatman GF/F filters. The filters were immediately frozen and stored at \( -18 \) \( ^\circ \mathrm{C} \) for later analysis. On return to the laboratory, the filters were dried at 60 \( ^\circ \mathrm{C} \) and sent to the University of California-Davis Stable Isotope Facility for analysis on a Europa Scientific Integra isotope ratio mass spectrometer. Specific uptake (\( v, \ \mathrm{h}^{-1} \)) and absolute uptake (\( \rho, \ \mu\mathrm{M}\ \mathrm{N}\ \mathrm{h}^{-1} \)) rates were calculated according to Dugdale and Goering (1967).

N fixation was measured using the high-precision, high-sensitivity tracer assay described by (Montoya et al., 1996, 2004). Briefly, 4-L acid-washed polycarbonate bottles were filled to overflowing with sample water and sealed with silicon septa caps. A gas-tight syringe was used to deliver 3 mL of \( ^{15}\mathrm{N}_2 \) (98 at% 15N, Sigma Chemicals). The sample bottles were gently mixed and placed in a deck incubator cooled with running seawater. Samples extracted from the DCM were shaded with neutral density screening to approximate in situ light levels, whereas surface samples were not screened. After an incubation period of 6–8 h, particulate material was collected by gentle vacuum filtration (\( <250 \) mmHg) through a filter array that separated the \( \geq 5 \)-μm size fraction onto a 5-μm Nitex screen and enabled the \( < 5 \)-μm size fraction to pass directly onto a 25 mm pre-combusted (500 \( ^\circ \mathrm{C} \), 4 h) glass fibre paper (Whatman GF/F). The \( \geq 5 \)-μm fraction was then rinsed off the Nitex filter with MilliQ ultrapurified water and onto a 25-mm GF/F paper. The filters were immediately frozen and stored at \( -20 \) \( ^\circ \mathrm{C} \) while at sea.

On return to the laboratory, samples were dried at 60 \( ^\circ \mathrm{C} \) and pressed into 5 × 9-mm tin capsules (Costech Analytical Technologies). The samples were analysed with a Roboprep elemental analyser coupled to a Europa PDZ Tracermass Ion Ratio Mass Spectrometer. System calibration was preformed with L-glutamic acid or radish (collegiate) standards. Analytical precision (two standard deviations) of the analyses were 0.5% for PN, 1% for PC, 0.3% for \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) and 0.15% \( \delta^{13}\mathrm{C} \). The specific uptake rate (\( v, \ \mathrm{h}^{-1} \)) and the absolute uptake rate (\( \rho, \ \mu\mathrm{mol}\ \mathrm{L}^{-1}\ \mathrm{h}^{-1} \)) for N fixation were determined according to the calculations shown in (Montoya et al., 1996).

Samples for phytoplankton taxonomy were collected at \( ^{15}\mathrm{N} \) uptake sites by collecting 500-mL whole seawater samples from the surface (bucket sample) and DCM depth. Each sample was stored in amber glass bottles and preserved with Lugol’s

</page>

<page number="3">

solution. The entire sample was settled and enumerated using an inverted light microscope according to the method of (Utermöhl, 1958). Samples were identified to class level only.

Phytoplankton pigment composition and concentration analysis were taken from 4-L sea-water samples at the surface and DCM. Each sample was collected onto a pre-combusted **(500 °C, 12 h) 25-mm Whatman GF/F filter and immediately stored on liquid N. Samples were sent for analysis at the CSIRO Marine Laboratories, Hobart, for high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) using methods analogous to those reported by Thompson et al., 2007. Phytoplankton taxa were separated using the CHEMTAX software (Mackey et al., 1996). The initial CHEMTAX pigment ratios were representative of equatorial species (Mackey et al., 1996) and provided strong agreement with the field data (<1% deviation for all pigments used). The following pigments were used for development of the CHEMTAX pigment ratios; peridinin, 19'-butanoyloxyfucoxanthin, fucoxanthin, 19'-hexanoyloxyfucoxanthin, prasinoxanthin, violaxanthin, diadinoxanthin, alloxanthin, violaxanthin, neoxanthin, lutein, zeaxanthin, chlorophyll b and chlorophyll a. Based on the pigments used in the matrix, the biomass proportion of classes; Prasinophyceae, Dinophyceae, Bacillariophyceae, Cryptophyceae, Haptophyceae, Chlorophyceae and the Cyanobacteria, Synechococcus, were determined.

The CHEMTAX pigment output data were analysed using Plymouth Routines in Multivariate Ecological Research (PRIMER v5) software to evaluate similarity and to create non-metric multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) plots.

3. Results

3.1. Physical water types

Major water masses were identified at each site in the present study on the basis of temperature–salinity (TS) characteristics in the surface 40 m, location of the station (relative to shore) and the current measurements using the shipborne ADCP. Using these techniques four major surface water masses were identified (see also Woo et al., 2006; Hanson et al., 2005a): (1) lower-salinity and warmer LC water along the shelf break close to the 200 m isobath; (2) colder, higher-salinity water associated with Capes Current on the continental shelf in depths <50 m; (3) colder, higher-salinity South Indian Central Water (SICW) located offshore of the LC, defined here as offshore Indian Ocean waters; and, (d) lower-salinity coastal water mass located adjacent the coast between Transects G and J (Fig. 1) and most likely influenced by freshwater run-off.

3.2. Chlorophyll a

The average surface chlorophyll a concentration across the study area was 0.20±0.13 mg chl a m^{-3} (SD), \( n = 42 \). There was no significant difference in surface concentration between sites grouped on the basis of location; those being the continental shelf, shelf break or open ocean (\( P = 0.664, \ n = 244 \)). Similarly, there was no evidence of variation in surface chlorophyll a concentration between transects from North to South (\( P = 0.108, \ n = 244 \)), determined by comparing data between 27°S–30°S, 30°S–33°S and 33°S–36°S; nor was there sufficient evidence of a linear relationship between latitude and chlorophyll a concentration (\( r = 0.09 \)).

A DCM was observed throughout the study area as elevated chlorophyll a concentrations near the seabed at sites on the continental shelf or as clear peaks within the water column at depths between 50 and 110 m. This was clearly evident from the representative fluorescence profiles shown in Fig. 2.

At the DCM the mean chlorophyll a concentration across the study area was 0.41±0.19 mg chl a m^{-3} (SE), \( n = 42 \). Comparison of the pooled surface chlorophyll concentration with the pooled DCM concentration revealed significantly higher levels at depth than at the surface (\( P < 0.001, \ n = 84 \)). The mean chlorophyll a concentration at the DCM was significantly higher at the open-ocean (0.526±0.175 mg chl a m^{-3}) and shelf-break (0.447±0.178 mg chl a m^{-3}) sites than those measured on the continental shelf (0.279±0.158 mg chl a m^{-3}; \( P < 0.001, \ n = 42 \)). Similarly, examination of the DCM in the major water masses revealed that the mean concentration in the LC (0.423±0.19 mg chl a m^{-3}) and offshore Indian Ocean waters (0.537±0.187 mg chl a m^{-3}) was significantly higher than those recorded at sites influenced by the Capes Current (0.277±0.038 mg chl a m^{-3}; \( P < 0.005, \ n = 42 \)). The distribution of chlorophyll a in the DCM was lower at northern latitudes (27°S–30°S; 0.301±0.171 mg chl a m^{-3}) compared with the southern latitudes (30°S–33°S; 0.459±0.21 and 33°S–36°S; 0.337±0.181 mg chl a m^{-3}); however, there was no evidence of a statistical difference at the \( \alpha = 0.05 \) level

3.3. DIN concentration

Nitrate concentration measured at sites on the continental shelf was typically below detection (<0.016 \( \mu \)M; Fig. 4). Similarly at the continental shelf break and beyond, nitrate concentrations were below detection in the surface 50 m. The nitricline (0.2 \( \mu \)M) was observed at sites with water depth >50 m and was typically deeper offshore than at the shelf break (Fig. 4). In the euphotic zone (\( \leq 140 \) m) at depths greater than the nitricline, nitrate was in the range of 0.5–2 \( \mu \)M. Nitrate concentration increased rapidly beyond 150 m depth to concentrations of around 30 \( \mu \)M. South of Cape Leeuwin on Transect N, the nitricline was shallower (~50 m) than elsewhere and concentrations >2 \( \mu \)M were evident in the euphotic zone (Fig. 4).

Ammonium concentration was typically below the analytical limits for detection (<0.016 \( \mu \)M) throughout the study area. Fewer than 10% of the 143 samples collected for ammonium analysis were above the detection limit. The distribution of ammonium in the euphotic zone was measured at the 100, 300 and 750 m isobaths on transect A (Fig. 5). These depth profiles indicate low ammonium concentration throughout the water column (below detection) with no discernable pattern with increasing depth.

3.4. N uptake

Based on the measured ammonium and nitrate levels and assuming a minimum concentration of 0.016 \( \mu \)M when levels were below the detection limit, the estimated trace additions represented ~1–25% enrichment. Considering that nearly all of the surface N uptake estimates were conducted on water samples where the concentrations of nitrate and ammonium were below detection, our uptake rates represent potential N uptake by phytoplankton in an enriched environment. Our estimates are therefore most likely representative of the maximum potential uptake, rather than ambient uptake rates in the surface waters.

3.5. \( f \)-ratio

Considering that the surface concentration of ammonium and nitrate was most often below the level of detection, the \( f \)-ratio was calculated based on equal amounts of nitrate and ammonium (0.016\( \mu \)M). Given that the absolute uptake values were not resolved at the surface, the calculated \( f \)-ratios represent potential, rather than absolute values. The \( f \)-ratio ranged from 0.11 to 0.95 at the surface and 0.07 and 0.93 at the DCM for all stations (Fig. 8). These data suggest high spatial variability of relative preference for nitrate over ammonium during the study. The mean \( f \)-ratio at the surface was 0.61 (0.18) on the shelf, 0.60 (0.24) at the shelf-break and 0.46 (0.28) at offshore sites (mean\( \pm \)SD). The mean \( f \)-ratio at the DCM was 0.47 (0.20) on the shelf, 0.66 (0.19) at the shelf break and 0.65 (0.18) at offshore sites. This indicates that N uptake was generally equitable between nitrate and ammonium, with a slight bias for nitrate uptake overall. There was an apparent shift from nitrate preference in the surface waters on the shelf and shelf break to ammonium preference at offshore sites; however, this was not statistically significant (Kruskall–Wallis \( P = 0.24, n = 43 \)). Similarly there was no significant difference in \( f \)-ratio between shelf, shelf-break and offshore sites at the DCM (Kruskall–Wallis \( P = 0.08, n = 41 \)) even though there was an apparent trend of nitrate preference at the shelf break and offshore.

3.7. Phytoplankton light microscopy data

Flagellates dominated surface and DCM phytoplankton community of the study area and were largely comprised of dinoflagellates and cryptophytes (Fig. 10B). Diatoms were found throughout the region, with highest proportions in offshore and shelf-break waters in the north (transect A) and on the shelf and shelf-break in the south (transect M). Only a small proportion of the total cell numbers were chlorophytes and chrysophytes, while cyanobacteria were largely absent from the study area.

The relative abundance of the major taxonomic groups was considerably different between the CHEMTAX and the direct cell counting methods. There are two major reasons why these differences were not unexpected: (1) cell counts are a measure of numerical abundance, while CHEMTAX is an estimate of abundance based on major pigment concentration, and (2) microscopy was restricted to cells >5 \( \mu \)m and therefore could not resolve the nano- and pico-plankton fractions, which formed a large fraction of the CHEMTAX biomass (Fig. 10A). Thus the direct counting method is biased toward large phytoplankton such as diatoms, whereas the CHEMTAX method is biased toward those taxa with high concentrations of pigment, yet may under-represent non-pigmented or lightly pigmented groups, such as dinoflagellates.

4. Discussion

In a previous summer cruise, Hanson et al. (2005a) demonstrated that the waters off the central-west coast of Australia were oligotrophic and areas of elevated phytoplankton productivity were associated with sporadic upwelling caused by wind driven processes and the dynamics of coastal currents. LC waters were devoid of N and had low primary productivity, whereas Ningaloo Current and northern Capes Current waters were more productive. The present study across continental shelf of the south-west of Australia suggest that the more southern LC waters off the west coast of Australia have strong similarities with the northern region of the LC. Inorganic N was undetected in the surface waters across the continental shelf and consequently the phytoplankton biomass was low (<20 mg chl \( a \) m\(^{-2}\)). N uptake rates were among the lowest values recorded (<15 nmol L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\)), comparable to oligotrophic regions of the Sargasso Sea (Glibert et al., 1988).

DCM have previously been described off the west Australian coast (Hanson et al., 2005a, 2007; Thompson et al., 2007) and appear to be a consistent feature of the biological oceanography. Typically DCM are associated with interplay between light and nutrient availability, density structure of the water, and losses to grazing (Cullen, 1982; Tett et al., 2002). In the present study nitrate uptake at the DCM was greater at the offshore Indian-Ocean sites (i.e. those offshore of the LC) than at the continental shelf break, which suggests that the elevated phytoplankton biomass in the DCM was fuelled by nitrate from the deeper waters. In addition, nitrate concentrations at the DCM were typically below analytical detection limits, and the high \( f \)-ratio suggests that nitrate and ammonium were utilised equally. These results indicate a dynamic physiological response that is clearly

integrating temporal and spatial variations in N availability. It was likely that, on average, phytoplankton in the DCM had access to the higher nitrate concentrations, being closer to sources of deep, nitrate rich water. The phytoplankton community would revert to ammonium uptake when nitrate was inaccessible or exhausted from the photic zone. The phytoplankton at the DCM must maintain, therefore, the ability to take up nitrate (i.e., significant cellular concentrations of the enzyme nitrate reductase, or NR) during periods when nitrate is unavailable, such as a time-lag

</page>

<page number="13">

between upwelling events. This would suggest that mixing events occur at a frequency closer to weekly rather than monthly. Longer gaps between nitrate mixing events would allow the deterioration of the NR uptake system critical in maintaining such a high \( f \)-ratio.

Similarly, spatial heterogeneity of integrated chlorophyll biomass observed in this study was related to N availability. For example, high integrated chlorophyll was observed at sites adjacent to Rottnest Island, near Perth Canyon, which has previously been associated with coastal upwelling (Gersbach et al., 1999; Pearce and Pattiaratchi, 1999; Rennie et al., 2007). These results were supported by high nitrate uptake, elevated \( f \)-ratios and a larger proportion of diatoms in the waters adjacent to Rottnest Island compared to other sites. Such observations are consistent with studies of upwelling zones, where diatoms dominate community composition when newly upwelled nitrate is available (Casas et al., 1997; Castro et al., 1994; Wilkerson and Dugdale, 1987). Similarly, the presence of low nitrate concentration combined with elevated uptake is characteristic of biological activity in recently upwelled waters (Dugdale et al., 1990).

However, upwelling on the south-west coast of Australia is sporadic and is predicted to only occur, across the whole shelf, between 5 and 9 times during the summer (Gersbach et al., 1999). The present study indicated that approximately 50% of measured N uptake was attributable to regenerated N in the form of ammonium. Thus, primary productivity in the south-west of Australia is most likely sustained by microbial regeneration of N, previously incorporated by the biological community after an upwelling event. Several studies have shown that when upwelling relaxes, the majority of newly produced organic matter is recycled through the microbial food web, redistributed as ammonium and ultimately reutilised by phytoplankton (Alvarez-Salgado et al., 1997, 2000; Bode et al., 2004). This process often manifests itself as a change in phytoplankton community structure, with nanoplankton and flagellates preferring regenerated N forms, and thereby increasing their relative proportions (Casas et al., 1997; Glibert, 1982; Lipschultz, 1995; Probyn, 1985). High diatom pigment concentration and cell counts on continental shelf sites suggest that diatoms were more prevalent in the Capes Current, which runs northward along the shelf (Gersbach et al., 1999; Pearce and Pattiaratchi, 1999) than in the LC or offshore Indian Ocean waters. The latter two water masses had phytoplankton communities dominated by nano and pico-plankton biomass and large proportions of dinoflagellates and cryptophytes. Owens et al. (1993) demonstrated a strong negative relationship between nitrate concentration and phytoplankton in the \( < 5 \)-µm size fraction. Our results concur, with smaller phytoplankton groups comprising the majority of phytoplankton biomass at sites at the shelf break and offshore Indian Ocean. The prevalence of cryptophytes throughout the region is consistent with oligotrophic waters, where small flagellates are favoured due to their large cell surface to volume ratio and enhanced nutrient uptake rates (Chisholm, 1992). The large number of dinoflagellates observed in our microscopy samples compared to very low concentrations of characteristic diagnostic pigments indicates that the community was largely represented by heterotrophic taxa. The high proportion of heterotrophic organisms, which may also include cryptophytes particularly at the DCM, is consistent with oligotrophic ecosystems where there is a shift from net autotrophy to net heterotrophy under nutrient limiting conditions (Jacobson and Anderson, 1996; Morey-Gaines and Elbrächter, 1987; Sanders et al., 2000).

Our results suggest a highly dynamic coastal phytoplankton community that has developed in response to patchy N supply. This is reflected in the \( f \)-ratio, which was amongst the most variable on record (Planas et al., 1999). Spatial variability of \( f \)-ratio indicates that the phytoplankton community were altering their community structure and physiological response relative to the supply of N. During the austral spring and summer the most likely sources of N for phytoplankton uptake include; regeneration, N-fixation or upwelling delivery from depth via some other episodic perturbation such as a mesoscale eddy (Thompson et al., 2007). Terrestrial N supply was likely to be insignificant during the dry season.

Several studies in upwelling zones have indicated that phytoplankton rely strongly on ammonium regeneration to maintain production throughout the year (Bode et al., 2004; Collos et al., 2003; Mengesha et al., 1999; Varela et al., 2003). The microbial food web plays an important role by recycling a large proportion of the organic material after an upwelling event (Bode et al., 2004). The relative distribution of N in the water column

</page>

<page number="14">

therefore is a function of the time from when the last upwelling event occurred. In the present study, ammonium was below analytical detection limits throughout the study area, yet our estimates of ammonium uptake were highly variable and included some significant uptake rates. It was likely that areas with large proportions of heterotrophic microplankton were supplying ammonium to the autotrophs via regeneration and excretion (Bidigare, 1983; Gaul et al., 1999; Probyn et al., 1990; Whitlege and Packard, 1971). High ammonium uptake is indicative of oligotrophic marine ecosystems (El-Sayed and Turner, 1977; Eppley et al., 1973, 1979; Sharp et al., 1980; Tett et al., 2002) and heterotrophic ammonium supply can account for up to 10–14% of the primary productivity (Bode et al., 2004; Probyn et al., 1990). Our results, which have shown regions with proportionally higher rates of ammonium uptake compared to nitrate uptake, and where ammonium was not detectable in the water column, suggest that ammonium regeneration and uptake are tightly coupled.

It is generally, agreed that the coastal and oceanic ecosystems are critically limited by N (Dugdale and Goering, 1967; Eppley and Sharp, 1975; Eppley et al., 1973; Ryther and Dunstan, 1971), which can lead to an increase of N2-fixing organisms (Paerl, 1990). The filamentous cyanobacterium Trichodesmium has long been considered the primary diazotrophic (N2-fixing) organism in the ocean (Karl et al., 2002). However, more recently the discovery of the enzyme nitrogenase in unicellular, coccoid cyanobacteria and bacteria in the North Pacific central gyre has suggested significant N2 fixation by nanoplankton and picoplankton was possible (Zehr et al., 2001). This was later demonstrated in the oligotrophic subtropical and tropical waters of the Pacific (Montoya et al., 2004). Currently little is known about the global distribution of these organisms, and their contribution to the marine N cycle is yet to be quantified (Arrigo, 2005). However, emerging data suggest that although the distribution of nanoplankton and picoplankton dizotrophs is spatially heterogenous, the rates of N2 fixation can contribute significantly to the total N pool (Montoya et al., 2004).

In N-limited oligotrophic ecosystems fixation can equal or exceed nitrate influx to the euphotic zone (Capone et al., 2005). However, in the present study N2 fixation was 2 orders of magnitude lower than ammonium and nitrate uptake. This was somewhat unexpected due to low rates of ammonium and nitrate uptake and proportionally high pico- and nano-plankton biomass throughout the study area. The low contribution of N2 fixation to total measured N uptake may result from nutrient limitation or co-limitation (Arrigo, 2005). N2 fixation has a strong Fe requirement for synthesis of the enzyme complex nitrogenase (Karl et al., 2002), and reports of Fe limitation of N2 fixation organisms are widespread (cf. Karl et al., 2002). Similarly, limitation by P may also reduce N2 fixation in oligotrophic waters (Voss et al., 2004). Low rates of N2 fixation observed in the present paper are most likely a reflection of severe nutrient impoverishment in the euphotic zone off the south-west coast of Australia. Significantly greater N2 fixation at the surface than at the DCM was most likely due to the high energy requirements of N2 fixation (Karl et al., 2002) and subsequent light limitation of this process at the DCM depth. Additionally, higher nitrate concentration at depth may have inhibited N2 fixation, particularly in Trichodesmium (Ohki et al., 1991). The spatial heterogeneity of N2 fixation observed in the current study indicates that the mechanisms of nutrient supply are the key drivers of N2 fixation off this coast. The sporadic N2 fixation demonstrated here suggests that dizotrophs are most likely reacting to pulsed nutrient supply, either through regeneration or to a lesser extent upwelling.

While only a relatively small fraction of the total measured N uptake could be attributed to N2 fixation in the present study during the austral summer, the presence of nano and pico-plankton dizotrophs off the south-west coast of Australia may indicate that these organisms are more active when the physico-chemical conditions are favourable. Upwelling off this coast has been demonstrated to be strongest during the summer due to upwelling-favourable SW prevailing wind (Gersbach et al., 1999). Nutrient loading to the euphotic zone is profoundly different during winter caused by an increase in terrestrial runoff and changes in wind strength and direction, which have been shown to suppress upwelling through stronger LC flow (Gersbach et al., 1999; Lourey et al., 2006). A better understanding of temporal variability of N2 fixation by nano- and pico-plankton dizotrophs is required to provide a more accurate estimate of their contribution to the N dynamics of the south-west Australian coastal waters.

Additionally, the contribution of N2 fixation by microplankton dizotrophs has not been quantified,

</page>

<page number="15">

even though this region is known to support blooms of chain-forming cyanobacteria from the genus *Trichodesmium*, considered the most prevalent microplankton N$_2$ fixer in the ocean (Carpenter et al., 2004). Senescent aggregation of these microplankton are often observed during the late summer and autumn in WA, such as a bloom estimated at 52,000 km$^2$ on the north-west coast of Australia (Wood, 1965). Considering that the coastal waters of WA are generally oligotrophic, *Trichodesmium* N$_2$ fixation could be an important contributor of new N to the ecosystem; however, quantification of their contribution to the N-pool is complicated by spatial and temporal variability. (One potential reason for the apparent absence of *Trichodesmium* in the oligotrophic waters off WA.)

Although N$_2$ fixation was not a significant source of new N in the study region during the 2-week cruise, the potential for N$_2$ fixation during other seasons may be viable. This was apparent from the HPLC diagnostic pigment results, which showed a large fraction of autotrophic biomass in cyanobacteria. Similarly, the absence of *Trichodesmium* in our microscopy samples suggests that the study may have under represented the N$_2$ fixation potential of the region. However, distribution of *Trichodesmium* may be limited in the oligotrophic waters off the west coast of Australia by seasonal differences in the temperature dependence of oxygen flux, respiration and N$_2$ fixation (Staal et al., 2003). The role of N$_2$ fixation for the biological N dynamics of these waters is therefore complicated by patchy distribution of N$_2$ fixing organisms in space and time, which can only be accurately assessed with greater temporal sampling resolution.

Absolute nitrate uptake at the DCM was not significantly different at the shelf-break sites compared with the continental-shelf and open-ocean sites (Mann–Whitney \( U, P = 0.11 \) and 0.288, respectively). \( ^{15} \)N\(_2\) specific uptake (\( \nu \)) and absolute uptake (\( \rho \); N\(_2\) fixation hereafter) rates were significantly higher for small phytoplankton (\(< 5 \mu\)m) than for phytoplankton greater than this size (Mann–Whitney \( U, P < 0.001 \) for both \( \nu \) and \( \rho \)). More than 90% of N\(_2\) fixation was measured in the small size fraction, and the majority of the large size fraction was below the limit of detection. Consequently, only the small size fraction was used for data analysis (Fig. 7). There was significantly higher N\(_2\) fixation at the surface than at the DCM at the \( \alpha = 0.1 \) level (Mann–Whitney \( U, P = 0.056, n = 69 \)). See discussions, stats, and author profiles for this publication at: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220023193 Fijación de nitrógeno por Cyanoprokaryota en la Reserva Ecológica El Edén, Q.R., México Article in Mexican Studies/Estudios Mexicanos · August 2003 DOI: 10.1525/msem.2003.19.2.277 CITATIONS 3 READS 80 2 authors: Rodrigo Vargas University of Delaware 217 PUBLICATIONS 11,869 CITATIONS SEE PROFILE Eberto Novelo Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México 66 PUBLICATIONS 792 CITATIONS SEE PROFILE Some of the authors of this publication are also working on these related projects: Representantiveness and Design of Environmental Observatory Networks View project FLUCAR View project MEXICAN STUDIES/ESTUDIOS MEXICANOS Fijación de nitrógeno por Cyanoprokaryota en la Reserva Ecológica El Edén, Q.R., México Rodrigo Vargas* Eberto Novelo Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México Acetylene reduction assay (ARA) was applied to determine the rate of nitrogen fixation by cyanoprokaryotes in a wetland in El Edén Ecological Reserve. The data obtained throughout a hydrological cycle showed both an increase of fixed nitrogen during wet periods and an important amount of nitrogen rate produced by non-heterocytic filamentous and colonial blue-green algae. The results support the importance of the contribution of algae to nutrient balance in the wetland ecosystem. Se realizó la prueba de reducción de acetileno para determinar la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno por cianoprokariotes en un humedal tropical de la Reserva Ecológica El Edén. Los datos obtenidos durante un ciclo hidrológico muestran tanto un incremento en el nitrógeno fijado durante el periodo de lluvias como una importante cantidad en la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno producida por algas verde-azules filamentosas no heterocitosa y coloniales. Los resultados respaldan la importancia de la contribución de las algas en el balance de nutrimentos en el humedal. La fijación de nitrógeno no simbiótica por algas cianoprokariotes (Cyanophyta—Cyanobacteria—Cyanoprokaryota) es un hecho bien es- * Trabajo presentado en el Simposio "The Lowland Maya Area: Three Millennia at the Human-Wildland Interface" celebrado en la Universidad de California, Riverside del 18 al 20 de enero de 2001. La realización de esta investigación fue posible gracias al apoyo de UC MEXUS—CONACYT y al proyecto CONACYT 25264-N. También agradecemos al Dr. David Romero del Centro de Investigación sobre Fijación de Nitrógeno de la UNAM por su asesoría y apoyo para la utilización del cromatógrafo de gases. A la Dra. Rosaluz Tavera por su valiosa contribución y comentarios al desarrollo de este proyecto. tablecido y la importancia de esta función en el ciclo biogeoquímico del nitrógeno en los ecosistemas puede resaltarse por la cantidad de nitrógeno que este tipo de algas aportan al suelo. En condiciones de anegación, como en humedales y arrozales, el aporte de nitrógeno al ecosistema puede alcanzar hasta 76.14 nanomoles de etileno por m² por hora (nm C₂H₄ m⁻² h⁻¹) durante la estación seca (Venkatamaran 1981). Para los humedales estacionales tropicales (no arrozales) no existen datos suficientes para comparar la eficiencia de fijación de nitrógeno por las cianoprokariotes pero se sabe que la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno es afectada, en organismos fotosintéticos, principalmente por el suplemento inadecuado de fotosintetatos al sistema de fijación de nitrógeno (Fay 1981). Factores como luz, temperatura, pH y oxígeno influyen directamente en el metabolismo de la fijación de nitrógeno y en el crecimiento de estos organismos (Stewart 1977). Así mismo, la radiación UVB afecta la productividad y disminuye la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno (Falcón-Álvarez 2000; Suresh Babu et al. 1998). Esta función la llevan a cabo organismos heterocitosos y no heterocitosos y puede observarse una separación espacial y temporal de la actividad de la enzima nitrogenasa (Bergman et al. 1997; Paerl et al. 1995; Quesada et al. 1998). En la Reserva Ecológica El Edén existen al menos cuatro meses en los que cerca de una tercera parte de su superficie se inunda. Estas condiciones ambientales dan origen a diversos humedales en donde se desarrollan varios tipos de vegetación en un gradiente relacionado con el tiempo de permanencia de la inundación y la profundidad del agua, desde selva baja subcaducifolia hasta cuerpos de agua permanentes. Uno de los componentes más importantes y menos conocidos de estos ecosistemas es el perifiton que crece en forma rápida y prácticamente cubre todo el suelo y las partes bajas de las plantas. El perifiton está constituido por una red de algas filamentosas y coloniales que forman una trama muy compleja. La productividad orgánica del perifiton en época de lluvias es, probablemente, la más importante de los humedales y desempeña un papel fundamental en el ciclaje de varios nutrimentos (Lampert y Sommer, 1997; MacDougal et al. 1997). Los crecimientos algales de los humedales de la Reserva Ecológica El Edén, están compuestos principalmente por algas de la división Cyanoprokaryota de tipo filamentoso y colonial. Para evaluar cómo es la participación de estas algas en el flujo de nitrógeno en los humedales se analizó la tasa de fijación de este nutriente por estos crecimientos algales durante un ciclo sequía—anegación. Se completa el análisis con una evaluación de la composición relativa de especies heterocitosas, coloniales y no fijadoras en cada caso. Figura 1. Localización de las parcelas estudiadas (1-4) para la evaluación de la fijación de nitrógeno. La zona sombreada señala la zona inundada. Area de estudio La Reserva Ecológica El Edén, Quintana Roo, es parte de la región de Yalahau al noreste de la península de Yucatán. Tiene una elevación entre 5 y 10 msnm y se localiza entre los 21°11"-21°14" N y los 87°10"-87°12" O. Se ubicaron parcelas de estudio (P1, P2, P3 y P4) en 4 sitios de vegetación vascular característica de la Reserva (Figura 1) y en las que los crecimientos de perifiton fueron siempre evidentes como costras compactas y hojuelas subaéreas durante la sequía y como tramas compactas durante el periodo anegado. Métodos Se visitó en tres ocasiones la Reserva durante 2000: abril (secas), agosto (principio de lluvias, periodo anegado) y noviembre (final de lluvias, periodo anegado). Se tomaron cuatro muestras de 1 cm\(^2\) del perifiton (blanco, más tres repeticiones) en cada una de las cuatro parcelas establecidas. Cuando fue posible se recolectó una muestra de agua y se hicieron submuestras dividiendo la costra en superior e inferior para determinar el porcentaje correspondiente de fijación en cada uno de los estratos. Este procedimiento se realizó porque la composición de especies varía tanto en la columna de agua (cuando hay anegación) como en el estrato superior e inferior del perifiton, lo que sugiere una división espacial en la fijación de nitrógeno. Las muestras se incubaron según la técnica de análisis para la reducción del acetileno (Weaver y Danso 1994) y se recolectaron muestras de la evolución de gases (5ml) cada seis horas para cubrir un ciclo de 24 horas. Las muestras de gases fueron almacenadas en Vacutainers y posteriormente analizadas en un cromatógrafo de gases (Varian 3300 y un integrador Varian 4290). Al mismo tiempo, se hicieron observaciones al microscopio de las muestras para obtener la proporción de las formas heterocitosas y no heterocitosas de cianoprokariotes, distinguiendo entre Nostocales y Stigonematales (filamentosas heterocitosas, FH), Oscillatoriales (filamentosas no heterocitosas, FnoH) y Chroococcales (coloniales, Cr) y se registraron como porcentaje de cobertura de un cm\(^2\). Resultados Se obtuvieron valores de la fijación de nitrógeno expresados como nm C\(_2\)H\(_4\) m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\). Los valores más altos que se obtuvieron corresponden al periodo de lluvias (Cuadro 1, Figura 2). Los estratos del perifiton aportan valores de fijación que se presentan como porcentaje del total obtenido para todo el crecimiento (Cuadro 2, Figura 3). La capa superior es la que produce el aporte mayor en la reducción, aunque resalta el hecho que en la parcela que mantiene menor cantidad de agua (P3), la participación proporcional de los estratos superiores e inferiores es semejante. Los datos obtenidos del agua de las parcelas también son notables pues corroboran el hecho de la pobreza de fitoplancton en El Edén (Novelo y Tavera, en prensa). Por otra parte, los resultados de la proporción de formas de Cyanoprokaryota muestran que las parcelas con mayor tasa de fijación (P4/agosto, P2/agosto y P1/noviembre), no necesariamente corresponden con aquellas con una composición principal de formas heterocitosas, como en la parcela 1 en la que las formas de tipo oscillatorial son los principales componentes del crecimiento (Cuadro 3). Discusión La importancia de la fijación no simbiótica de nitrógeno en sistemas de agua dulce radica en su condición de factor limitante en muchos de estos ambientes (Wetzel 2001). Los principales componentes de la comunidad de algas del perifiton que encontramos en El Edén son las Cyanoprokaryota, que alcanzan cerca del 90% de la cobertura del crecimiento algal. Esta característica no es única de El Edén ya que los tapetes de cianoprokariotes son componentes importantes de los humedales oligotróficos del Caribe (Rejmánková y Komárková 2000). Las formas constitutivas, dentro de este grupo, cambian en las distintas épocas de recolección lo que podría reflejarse en la diferencia en la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno. En El Edén, durante las periodos de sequía (marzo-mayo), el metabolismo de las algas disminuye, se forman estructuras de resistencia y se reduce la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno. Cuando comienzan las lluvias se hidrata el perifiton, el metabolismo algal se activa y se observa un aumento en la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno. En el periodo de mayor anegación es cuando se registra la mayor tasa de fijación de nitrógeno, por ejemplo en las parcelas 2, 3 y 4 en agosto y en la parcela 1 en noviembre. Cuando el nivel de agua disminuye en las parcelas 3 y 4 (noviembre) y el perifiton se encuentra como una costra humedecida, el metabolismo de la fijación disminuye. La presencia de agua, la composición de especies y el cambio en la actividad metabólica después del periodo de sequía es lo que determina el aumento en la fijación de nitrógeno en agosto. Al final de lluvias el estado metabólico del perifiton es distinto ya que aparecen estructuras de resistencia lo que implica una disminución en el metabolismo y por tanto disminuye la fijación de nitrógeno. Este ciclo concuerda con lo discutido por Fay (1981) para los ambientes con ciclos hídricos de sequía y anegación. La fijación de nitrógeno está distribuida verticalmente en la estructura del perifiton (estratos superior e inferior) y en la mayoría de los ca- sos existe una participación similar de cada estrato. Tomando en cuenta que la capa superior está formada principalmente por filamentos de cianoprokariotes heterocitosas y que en la inferior aparecen formas coloniales y filamentosas no heterocitosas, es notable que el aporte de estas capas inferiores sea relativamente importante. La capa superior está formada por varias especies de Scytonema con vainas gruesas y pigmentadas. Esta capa puede servir de filtro a las altas temperaturas, la desecación y como derivado, a mantener temperaturas relativamente menos altas. Estas condiciones favorecerían una condición de baja concentración de oxígeno en las capas inferiores y por tanto la nitrogenasa presente en las células no heterocitosas podría funcionar durante mayor tiempo. Una proporción claramente definida de algas heterocitosas en la estructura del perifiton analizado, durante el periodo de anegación (agosto—noviembre), podría servir como evidencia de que las formas no heterocitosas presentes en la parcela 3 durante todo el año, son las responsables de cerca de la mitad del nitrógeno fijado en ese lugar, sin embargo este hecho deberá ser corroborado con la evaluación de la tasa de fijación en cultivos uniaigales de cada una de las especies predominantes en el perifiton. El Edén presenta un intervalo de fijación de nitrógeno que va desde 2.18 hasta 63.94 nm C2H4 m^{-2} h^{-1} a lo largo del año que puede ser comparado con la tasa de fijación registrada en los estromatolitos de Cyanoprokaryota del lago de Alchichica, Puebla, 0.24 a 25.72 nm C2H4 m^{-2} h^{-1} (Falcón-Alvarez 2000), con la encontrada por Stewart y colaboradores (1978) en varios hábitats de Escocia, que varía entre los 0.02 y 15.7 nm C2H4 m^{-2} h^{-1}, con los valores registrados por Venkatamaran (1981) para los arrozales de la India (76.14 nm C2H4 m^{-2} h^{-1}) y con los de Senegal donde la tasa de fijación varía de 0 a 60 nm C2H4 m^{-2} h^{-1} (Buresh et al. 1980). Esta comparación hace evidente que la producción de nitrógeno fijado por cyanoprokariotes en El Edén es una de las más altas para este tipo de ecosistemas naturales. Los datos obtenidos refuerzan la importancia del papel del perifiton en el ciclo biogeoquímico del nitrógeno, en los humedales en general y en los humedales tropicales en particular, pero sobre todo aclaran el papel de las cianoprokariotes del perifiton en los humedales tropicales cársticos con suelos poco profundos, como en El Edén, donde se mantiene una comunidad vegetal muy productiva. Nitrogen enrichment during decomposition of mangrove leaf litter in an east African coastal lagoon (Kenya): Relative importance of biological nitrogen fixation A.F. WOITCHIK1, B. OHOWA2, J.M. KAZUNGU2, R.G. RAO1, L. GOEYENS1 & F. DEHAIRS1 1Laboratory for Analytical Chemistry (Address for correspondence), Vrije Universiteit Brussel, Pleinlaan 2, B-1050 Brussels, Belgium; 2Kenya Marine & Fisheries Research Institute, P. O. Box 81651, Mombasa, Kenya Accepted 28 April 1997 Key words: decomposition, leaf litter, mangrove, nitrogen fixation Abstract. In situ decomposition of senescent leaves of two abundant mangrove species (Rhizophora mucronata Lamarck and Ceriops tagal (Perr) C.B. Rob), enrichment of nitrogen and activity of dinitrogen fixing bacteria during decomposition were investigated during both rainy and dry seasons in a tropical coastal lagoon (Gazi, Kenya). Rates of leaf decomposition were higher for R. mucronata than for C. tagal and were highest, for both species, during rainy season. Rates of decomposition, expressed as percentage dry mass loss, over a decomposition period of 50 days was: C. tagal (rainy season), 69%; C. tagal (dry season), 27%; R. mucronata (rainy season), 98%; and R. mucronata (dry season), 48%. High rainfall and diurnal tidal inundation appear to enhance the leaf decomposition process. Maximum rates of nitrogen fixation were 380 nmol N2 h^{-1} g^{-1} dw for C. tagal (rainy season), 78 nmol N2 h^{-1} g^{-1} dw for C. tagal (dry season), 390 nmol N2 h^{-1} g^{-1} dw for R. mucronata (rainy season) and 189 nmol N2 h^{-1} g^{-1} dw for R. mucronata (dry season). Although N2 fixation rates were highest during rainy season, total nitrogen immobilised in the leaves was highest during the dry season. Biological nitrogen fixation can account for between 13 to 21% of the maximum nitrogen immobilised in the decaying mangrove leaves. Nitrogen fixation, as a source of allochthonous nitrogen, sustains a nitrogen input to the mangrove ecosystem, which adds significantly to the nitrogen input through leaf litterfall. Introduction Mangroves are important sites of primary production and contribute considerable quantities of organic matter, primarily as leaves, to adjacent waters and sediments (Benner et al. 1986). Only a small percentage of mangrove leaves is consumed directly by terrestrial grazing animals (Lee et al. 1990), whereas mangrove detritus constitutes a large carbon reservoir potentially available to the estuarine food web (Benner & Hodson 1985; Tam et al. 1990). The pioneering work of W.E. Odum and E.J. Heald in southern Florida in the late 1960’s documented the importance of detritus-based food chains for near shore secondary production in mangrove-dominated estuaries (Odum & Heald 1975; Robertson et al. 1992). The C:N ratio of mangrove litter has been considered as an indicator of its nutritional value (Fell et al. 1984). Furthermore it has been well documented that the nutritional value of mangrove litter increased through nitrogen enrichment during microbial decomposition (Fell et al. 1984; Newell et al. 1984; Van der Valk & Attiwill 1984; Mann & Steinke 1992). Microbial carbon respiration can contribute to the relative nitrogen enrichment of plant litter as suggested by Morris & Lajtha (1986). White & Howes (1994) estimated that the microbial biomass can contribute 20 to 25% of the leaf litter nitrogen of Spartina. In addition, the following mechanisms for nitrogen accumulation in detritus were proposed (Rice 1982): (1) after initial leaching from fresh detritus, microbial enzymes depolymerize the detritus substrate producing reactive carbohydrates, phenols, small peptides, and amino acids; (2) the carbohydrates and phenols condense with polypeptides and amino acids to produce nitrogenous geopolymers; (3) microbes associated with detritus assimilate nitrogen from an external source for protein (including exoenzyme) synthesis; (4) exoenzymes exuded by microbes condense with reactive carbohydrates and phenols in the humifying detritus. If the condensation products are not easily solubilized in sea water, the detritus particle becomes enriched with humic nitrogen. A central question is: what are the possible significant sources of external nitrogen for leaf litter nitrogen enrichment? One of the sources of external nitrogen to leaf detritus can be the water column (Rice & Tenore 1981; Rice 1982; Steinke & Charles 1986). In addition, biological nitrogen fixation has been suggested as a possible source of nitrogen (Fell et al. 1984; Van der Valk & Attiwill 1984; Twilley et al. 1986; Boto & Robertson 1990). Several authors have reported the presence of different types of nitrogen-fixing micro-organisms in sediments and decaying leaves of mangroves (Zuberer & Silver 1978; Mann & Steinke 1992). Gotto and Taylor (1976) attributed two thirds of nitrogenase activity associated with decomposing R. mangle leaves to photosynthetic bacteria and non-heterocystous blue-green algae. Facultative or strictly anaerobic heterotrophic bacteria account for the remaining nitrogenase activity. Using natural carbon isotope abundance Rao et al. (1994) showed that mangrove leaves represent a major source of organic carbon to the mangrove sediments of Gazi. Moreover, they observed a tenfold decrease in C:N ratio from senescent leaves (C:N = 200) to the sediments (C:N = 22), suggesting significant nitrogen enrichment during leaf decomposition. Hemminga et al. (1994) observed that seston from Gazi lagoon consists largely of mangrove derived particulate organic matter having a low C:N ratio (6.5 to 10) relative to senescent mangrove leaves, and they suggest that the mangrove derived organic particles have gone through intensive processing during outwelling from the mangrove and trapping in the seagrass zone. The studies of Rao et al. (1994) and Hemminga et al. (1994) have emphasized the importance of mangrove derived detritus in Gazi lagoon and stress the need for assessing the role and fate of mangrove litter in the lagoonal ecosystem. The aims of the present study were to quantify nitrogen enrichment during leaf decomposition, to assess the contribution of biological nitrogen fixation (as a microbial pathway of incorporating inorganic nitrogen from the atmosphere), to assess the seasonal variability of these processes and to quantify the nitrogen input through mangrove litterfall into the lagoonal ecosystem. Material and methods Site description Gazi is situated 50 km south of Mombasa, Kenya (Figure 1). Large parts of the lagoon are covered with seagrass beds and a mangrove swamp of 6.6 km\(^2\). Two major tidal creeks are leading out of the mangrove forest and only the western creek receives fresh water from the river Kidogoweni. Eight mangrove species are found, with dominant species being Rhizophora mucronata locally mixed with Bruguiera gymnorrhiza and Ceriops tagal. Stands of Sonneratia alba and Avicennia marina are found along the creek fringes (Gallin et al. 1989). On higher areas, Ceriops tagal appears in monospecific stands (Hemminga et al. 1994; Rao et al. 1994). The area is influenced by two monsoonal regimes: from October to March by the northeast monsoon and from March to October by the southeast monsoon (McClanahan 1988). Rainfall is highest in the period from May to July during southeast monsoon (Table 1 and McClanahan 1988; Ruwa 1993). Two fieldwork plots (20 m by 20 m) were selected to conduct litterfall measurements and decomposition experiments. The plots were chosen amidst vegetation zones representative of the Gazi mangrove. The first one is a pure Ceriops tagal plot developed on sandy sediment and inundated only during spring tide events. These events extend over six days and occur twice a month. The second plot is located within a pure Rhizophora mucronata vegetation zone developed on muddy sediment and is inundated twice a day. The tidal amplitude is approximately 3 m. Three half Rhizophora leaves or five half Ceriops leaves were weighed to within 0.001 g (leaf weights ranged between 1.11 and 4.11 g) and packed into nylon litter bags (10 cm × 20 cm) with mesh size of 2 mm. This mesh size is too small for significant loss of small leaf particles but is large enough to allow for microbial colonisation and passage of small benthic invertebrates (Gallardo & Merino 1992). The remaining leaf halves were kept for analysis of initial C and N content. In the selected Rhizophora and Ceriops plots, 36 to 54 litter bags were tied with nylon rope to the aerial roots of the trees. Empty litter bags were set out as well to serve as blanks for the nitrogen fixation measurements. A first series of experiments was conducted during the rainy season (May till July 1991), and a second one during the dry season (December 1991 till February 1992). A third experiment was designed to investigate differences between Rhizophora leaves that were continuously submerged in the creek and samples kept in the Rhizophora plot and affected by daily tidal inundation. Finally, a fourth experiment was carried out during rainy season (June 1992) in the Rhizophora plot to study leaf decomposition during the first 15 days with a higher time resolution. Triplicate litter bag samples were collected randomly, together with one blank sample, at different time intervals from day 1 till the end of the experiments. In the Mombasa laboratory they were kept one night in the dark, at laboratory temperature (25 °C) and humidity before being assessed for nitrogen fixation. Prior to nitrogen fixation measurements, the litter bags were gently washed with tap water to remove attached sediment particles (Newell et al. 1984; Twilley et al. 1986). After nitrogen fixation measurements, leaves were removed from the litter bags, dried at 80 °C to constant weight, weighed and stored for later C and N analysis. C and N content analysis The dry leaves were ground into fine powder after pre treatment with liquid nitrogen to increase their brittleness. Total organic carbon and nitrogen were measured with a Carlo Erba NA 1500 elemental analyser on weighed aliquots of approximately 3 mg. Acetanilide (C = 71.03%, N = 10.36%) was used for standardization. Nitrogen fixation measurements Nitrogen fixation activity was measured according to the acetylene reduction technique of Hardy et al. (1968). Within 20 hours after sampling the triplicate litter bags were incubated together in the same gas tight plexiglas enclosure (diameter, 20 cm; height, 25 cm), fitted with a gas sampling device. Incubations were done at 25 °C, in aerobiose. With each run, a blank sample (litterbag without leaves) was incubated separately. Acetylene was injected into the enclosures to a final concentration of 10% in volume. Ethane (100 \( \mu l \)) was injected as an internal standard. Reduction of acetylene into ethylene was monitored during 8 h with hourly analyses of 100 \( \mu l \) gas samples using a Varian model 3300 gas chromatograph. Peak areas were measured with a Varian model 4400 integrator. Acetylene, ethylene and ethane were calibrated using a mixture of pure calibration gases. The acetylene reduction rates were converted to rates of nitrogen fixation using the theoretical conversion factor of three acetylene molecules for one N\(_2\) molecule (Turner & Gibson 1980). Statistics Statistical analysis through one way ANOVA at 95% confidence interval and further analysis through Fisher PLSD (Protected Least Square Design) and Scheffe F-test were performed by means of a Macintosh computing package “Statview II”. Discussion Leaf decomposition The decay rate of plant litter can be affected by litter quality and by ambient physico-chemical conditions such as temperature, oxygen concentration and humidity (Melillo et al. 1984). Several authors (Melillo et al. 1984; Twilley et al. 1986; Robertson et al. 1992) have reported a close relationship between decay rate and initial leaf nitrogen concentration, with faster degradation associated with higher nitrogen content. Our observations do not confirm this. We observed highest decomposition rates for both species of mangrove during the rainy season when the C:N ratios are highest. Indeed, the mean initial C:N ratios for dry season (178 for Ceriops and 167 for Rhizophora) were significantly different (\( p < 0.05 \)) from the mean initial C:N ratios for the rainy season (256 for Ceriops and 206 for Rhizophora). Other factors such as the ratio of lignin to nitrogen has been shown to correlate well with mass loss rates for non-leguminous litter (Constantinides & Fownes 1994). In the present study we did not analyse for lignin content of the mangrove leaves. Some authors (Twilley et al. 1986; Steinke & Ward 1987; Robertson et al. 1992) have emphasised the importance of the frequency of tidal inundation on the rate of leaf decomposition with higher rates associated with increased tidal frequency. Our results show a similar trend. The C. tagal plot is situated at a higher intertidal range and is inundated only during spring tides. Leaf degradation in the C. tagal plot is slower than in the R. mucronata plot that is situated at a low intertidal range and subject to diurnal tidal inundation. However, for R. mucronata, comparison of the decomposition rate of continuously submerged leaves with the rate of leaves kept within the Rhizophora plot and submerged twice a day, showed slightly but significantly lower (\( p < 0.05 \)) decomposition rates for continuously submerged leaves (Figure 2). Similar results were obtained in South Africa by Mann & Steinke (1992) for leaves of A. marina and in Thailand by Boonruang (1984) for leaves of R. apiculata. The latter author attributes the difference to the presence of a larger number of micro-organisms (fungi and bacteria) and grazers within the forest. Very few of the authors who studied mangrove litter decomposition paid attention to the seasonal variation of decomposition rates. Twilley et al. (1986) and Flores-Verdugo et al. (1987) observed higher degradation rates associated with the rainy season. Steinke and Ward (1987) observed higher degradation rates during the warm season but did not describe rainfall. In our study, decomposition was faster during the rainy season despite a lower air temperature (Table 1). Furthermore, a large difference in decay rates of R. mucronata leaves was observed between rainy seasons of two successive years. Leaf decomposition during the period from May till July 1991 was faster than during June 1992 and rainfall in May and June was about twice as high in 1991 as in 1992, while there were no significant differences in air temperature between both rainy seasons (Table 1). It may be, therefore, that rainfall is more important than air temperature and that higher rainfall enhances leaf decomposition rates. The effect of rainfall on decomposition rates, could result from the subsequent supply of inorganic nutrients through freshwater discharge in the lagoonal waters (Kazungu et al. 1993). Indeed, during the rainy season, nitrate concentrations ranged from 0.2 to 1.7 \( \mu \)mol l\(^{-1} \) and ammonium from 0.1 to 0.9 \( \mu \)mol l\(^{-1} \) between high and low tide. During dry season, on the contrary, there is no significant freshwater discharge in the system and nitrate and ammonium concentrations remain below 0.2 \( \mu \)mol l\(^{-1} \) (Kazungu et al. 1993, and unpublished results). Higher nutrient content of the water column during rainy season together with a higher relative humidity, could sustain a rapid initial microbial colonisation of the leaves. *Nitrogen fixation and nitrogen immobilisation* Maximum nitrogen fixation rates for *Ceriops* amounted to 78 and 380 nmol N\(_2\) h\(^{-1}\) g\(^{-1}\) for dry and rainy season respectively. For *Rhizophora*, maximum nitrogen fixation rates were 125 and 390 nmol N\(_2\) h\(^{-1}\) g\(^{-1}\) for dry and rainy season respectively. The values we observed for the dry season are similar to the values reported by others, while our values for the rainy season are larger than those reported elsewhere. Examples of literature values for nitrogen fixation associated with decaying mangrove litter are, for *R. mangle*: 30 nmol N\(_2\) h\(^{-1}\) fresh weight g\(^{-1}\) (Zuberer & Silver 1978) and for *A. marina*: 12 nmol N\(_2\) h\(^{-1}\) g\(^{-1}\) (Hicks & Silvester 1985); 347 nmol N\(_2\) h\(^{-1}\) g\(^{-1}\) (Mann & Steinke 1992); 156 nmol N\(_2\) h\(^{-1}\) g\(^{-1}\) (Van der Valk & Attiwill 1984). To evaluate the contribution of nitrogen fixation to the immobilisation of nitrogen in mangrove leaves when any, we integrated the nitrogen fixation rates over time. Nitrogen fixation values reported in Tables 2, 3, 4, 5, were corrected for mass loss and expressed per day. We arbitrarily decided N\(_2\) fixation to apply only between sunrise and sunset (12 h, Gotto & Taylor 1976). We assumed these corrected nitrogen fixation rates applied throughout each period comprised between midpoints of successive litterbag sampling events. These time-weighted N\(_2\) fixation values were summed, and these integrated values (in \( \mu \)g N g\(^{-1}\)) were compared with the difference (N gain) between Nt, corrected for mass loss, and No (Nt and No from Tables 2, 3, 4, 5). During the 1991 rainy season, after the first days of decomposition, mass losses exceeded the input of external nitrogen in the decaying leaves of both species of mangroves and therefore no nitrogen immobilisation was observed (Figures 4a and 4c). For the 1991–1992 dry season, at maximum immobilisation of nitrogen in the C. tagal leaves (70 days, 1626 \( \mu \)g N g\(^{-1}\)), integrated nitrogen fixation reached 208 \( \mu \)g N g\(^{-1}\) and could account for 13% of the nitrogen immobilised (Figure 4b). At maximum immobilisation of nitrogen in the leaves of R. mucronata (54 days, 4273 \( \mu \)g N g\(^{-1}\)), integrated nitrogen fixation reached 887 \( \mu \)g N g\(^{-1}\), and could account for 21% of the nitrogen immobilised in the leaves (Figure 4d). In general, these calculated values are lower than the results of Van der Valk & Attiwill (1984) who estimated that nitrogen fixation could supply 40 to 64% of the nitrogen enrichment of A. marina leaves during decomposition. Nitrogen input to the mangrove ecosystem From litterfall data for the Rhizophora and Ceriops plots in Gazi (Slim & Gwada 1993) and initial nitrogen content of leaf litter (this study) we calculated the nitrogen input to the lagoonal ecosystem through leaf shedding to range between 0.86 and 13.98 mg N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Table 6), depending on mangrove species and season. To calculate the additional amount of allochtonous nitrogen resulting from nitrogen fixation during mangrove leaf decay, we multiplied the N\(_2\) fixation values integrated over the decomposition period by the litterfall values (Table 6). Thus the additional amount of allochtonous nitrogen that can be imported into the mangrove sediments, represented between 0.28 and 4.15 mg N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Table 6). However, it is probable that nitrogen fixation is not restricted to the decaying leaf but occurs also on small detrital particles accumulated in the sediments (Table 6). We obtained some preliminary results concerning nitrogen fixation associated with sediments. During the dry season (February 1994) we measured an activity of 2.3 mg N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) for sediments of the Ceriops plot and of 0.8 mg N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) for sediments of the Rhizophora plot. The importance of the allochtonous nitrogen input associated with nitrogen fixation in the sediments is presently under further investigation and natural nitrogen isotope abundance will be analysed to evaluate directly the percentage of incorporated nitrogen derived from biological nitrogen fixation (e.g. Mariotti et al. 1992). The data above suggest that nitrogen fixation can contribute significantly to the observed nitrogen enrichment of organic detritus between its input as mangrove leaf litter and its accumulation in the sediments. However other sources of allochthonous nitrogen, such as the inputs of nutrient rich freshwater through rainfall, river discharge and ground water seepage, exist and need to be taken into account. * data from Slim & Gwada (1993) Conclusion In this study of a tropical mangrove ecosystem we focused on the seasonal variation of: (1) in situ decomposition of senescent mangrove leaves; (2) immobilisation of nitrogen during leaf decomposition and (3) nitrogen fixation associated with the decaying leaves. Rates of leaf decomposition were higher for R. mucronata than for C. tagal and were highest, for both species, during the rainy season. High rainfall and a diurnal alternation of drying and wetting of the leaves by tidal inundation appear to enhance leaf decomposition rates. During rainy season, mass loss exceeded the external input of nitrogen after a maximum of 13 days of decomposition. More nitrogen was immobilised in the leaves of both species of mangroves during the dry season than during the rainy season. Rates of nitrogen fixation were highest during the rainy season for C. tagal. During the dry season, rates of nitrogen fixation were higher for R. mucronata than for C. tagal. Biological nitrogen fixation accounted for between 13 and 21% of the maximum nitrogen immobilisation in the decomposing leaves, indicating that nitrogen fixation, although representing a significant source of allochtonous nitrogen to the mangrove ecosystem, is not the major nitrogen source. Nitrogen enrichment during decomposition of mangrove leaf litter in an east African coastal lagoon (Kenya): Relative importance of biological nitrogen fixation

A.F. WOITCHIK1, B. OHOWA2, J.M. KAZUNGU2, R.G. RAO1, L. GOEYENS1 & F. DEHAIRS1
1Laboratory for Analytical Chemistry (Address for correspondence), Vrije Universiteit Brussel, Pleinlaan 2, B-1050 Brussels, Belgium; 2Kenya Marine & Fisheries Research Institute, P. O. Box 81651, Mombasa, Kenya

Accepted 28 April 1997

Key words: decomposition, leaf litter, mangrove, nitrogen fixation

Abstract. In situ decomposition of senescent leaves of two abundant mangrove species (Rhizophora mucronata Lamarck and Ceriops tagal (Perr) C.B. Rob), enrichment of nitrogen and activity of dinitrogen fixing bacteria during decomposition were investigated during both rainy and dry seasons in a tropical coastal lagoon (Gazi, Kenya). Rates of leaf decomposition were higher for R. mucronata than for C. tagal and were highest, for both species, during rainy season. Rates of decomposition, expressed as percentage dry mass loss, over a decomposition period of 50 days was: C. tagal (rainy season), 69%; C. tagal (dry season), 27%; R. mucronata (rainy season), 98%; and R. mucronata (dry season), 48%. High rainfall and diurnal tidal inundation appear to enhance the leaf decomposition process. Maximum rates of nitrogen fixation were 380 nmol N2 h^{-1} g^{-1} dw for C. tagal (rainy season), 78 nmol N2 h^{-1} g^{-1} dw for C. tagal (dry season), 390 nmol N2 h^{-1} g^{-1} dw for R. mucronata (rainy season) and 189 nmol N2 h^{-1} g^{-1} dw for R. mucronata (dry season). Although N2 fixation rates were highest during rainy season, total nitrogen immobilised in the leaves was highest during the dry season. Biological nitrogen fixation can account for between 13 to 21% of the maximum nitrogen immobilised in the decaying mangrove leaves. Nitrogen fixation, as a source of allochthonous nitrogen, sustains a nitrogen input to the mangrove ecosystem, which adds significantly to the nitrogen input through leaf litterfall.

Introduction

Mangroves are important sites of primary production and contribute considerable quantities of organic matter, primarily as leaves, to adjacent waters and sediments (Benner et al. 1986). Only a small percentage of mangrove leaves is consumed directly by terrestrial grazing animals (Lee et al. 1990), whereas mangrove detritus constitutes a large carbon reservoir potentially available to the estuarine food web (Benner & Hodson 1985; Tam et al. 1990). The pioneering work of W.E. Odum and E.J. Heald in southern Florida in the late 1960’s documented the importance of detritus-based food chains for

maximum value of 239% (day 54). Afterwards, the immobilisation of nitrogen decreased and at day 70, nitrogen loss overtook nitrogen gain.

During both seasons, significantly more nitrogen (\( p < 0.05 \)) was immobilised in \( R. mucronata \) leaves than in \( C. tagal \) ones. Significantly more nitrogen (\( p < 0.05 \)) was immobilised in \( R. mucronata \) leaves kept on the forest floor compared to continuously submerged leaves (data not shown).

Nitrogen fixation

Maximum rates of nitrogen fixation were observed during or at the end of the first month of decomposition (Tables 2, 3, 4, 5).

During the 1991 rainy season, we observed a maximal nitrogen fixation rate of 380 nmol N\(_2\) h\(^{-1}\) g\(^{-1}\) after 32 days of decomposition for \( C. tagal \). \( R. mucronata \) exhibited peak activity of 390 nmol N\(_2\) h\(^{-1}\) g\(^{-1}\) after 16 days and a decrease to a zero value after 36 days due to almost complete decomposition
pages.14:
For the 1991–1992 dry season, at maximum immobilisation of nitrogen in the C. tagal leaves (70 days, 1626 \( \mu \)g N g\(^{-1}\)), integrated nitrogen fixation reached 208 \( \mu \)g N g\(^{-1}\) and could account for 13% of the nitrogen immobilised (Figure 4b). At maximum immobilisation of nitrogen in the leaves of R. mucronata (54 days, 4273 \( \mu \)g N g\(^{-1}\)), integrated nitrogen fixation reached 887 \( \mu \)g N g\(^{-1}\), and could account for 21% of the nitrogen immobilised in the leaves (Figure 4d). In general, these calculated values are lower than the results of Van der Valk & Attiwill (1984) who estimated that nitrogen fixation could supply 40 to 64% of the nitrogen enrichment of A. marina leaves during decomposition.

Nitrogen input to the mangrove ecosystem

From litterfall data for the Rhizophora and Ceriops plots in Gazi (Slim & Gwada 1993) and initial nitrogen content of leaf litter (this study) we calculated the nitrogen input to the lagoonal ecosystem through leaf shedding to range between 0.86 and 13.98 mg N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Table 6), depending on mangrove species and season. To calculate the additional amount of allochtonous nitrogen resulting from nitrogen fixation during mangrove leaf decay, we multiplied the N\(_2\) fixation values integrated over the decomposition period by the litterfall values (Table 6). Thus the additional amount of allochtonous nitrogen that can be imported into the mangrove sediments, represented between 0.28 and 4.15 mg N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Table 6). However, it is probable that nitrogen fixation is not restricted to the decaying leaf but occurs also on small detrital particles accumulated in the sediments (Table 6). We obtained some preliminary results concerning nitrogen fixation associated with sediments. During the dry season (February 1994) we measured an activity of 2.3 mg N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) for sediments of the Ceriops plot and of 0.8 mg N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) for sediments of the Rhizophora plot. The importance of the allochtonous nitrogen input associated with nitrogen fixation in the sediments is presently under further investigation and natural nitrogen isotope abundance will be analysed to evaluate directly the percentage of incorporated nitrogen derived from biological nitrogen fixation (e.g. Mariotti et al. 1992).

The data above suggest that nitrogen fixation can contribute significantly to the observed nitrogen enrichment of organic detritus between its input as mangrove leaf litter and its accumulation in the sediments. However other sources of allochthonous nitrogen, such as the inputs of nutrient rich freshwater through rainfall, river discharge and ground water seepage, exist and need to be taken into account.

Rates of leaf decomposition were higher for R. mucronata than for C. tagal and were highest, for both species, during the rainy season. High rainfall and a diurnal alternation of drying and wetting of the leaves by tidal inundation appear to enhance leaf decomposition rates. During rainy season, mass loss exceeded the external input of nitrogen after a maximum of 13 days of decomposition.
