Dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA) seasonally dominates NO\(_3^-\) reduction pathways in an anthropogenically impacted sub-tropical coastal lagoon

Rebecca J. Bernard · Behzad Mortazavi · Alice A. Kleinhuizen

Received: 29 May 2014 / Accepted: 28 May 2015 / Published online: 17 June 2015
© Springer International Publishing Switzerland 2015

Abstract  Sediments have an important role in nutrient dynamics by providing sites for denitrification, which, in conjunction with nitrogen (N) fixation and other processes such as dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA), can regulate ecosystem N availability. Little Lagoon, Alabama, USA, is affected by anthropogenic perturbations and has N inputs from nitrate (NO\(_3^-\))-contaminated submarine groundwater discharge. N cycle pathways (N-fixation, denitrification, anammox, and DNRA) and benthic fluxes were measured at three sites over a year to investigate the hypothesis that DNRA, by producing ammonium (NH\(_4^+\)) as a dissimilatory end product of NO\(_3^-\) reduction, was a significant process retaining bioavailable fixed N in Little Lagoon. DNRA was found to be an important NO\(_3^-\) reduction pathway, especially in the summer months (study average: 52.1 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1} \)) compared to denitrification (study average 7.7 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1} \)). Sulfidic sediments during the majority of the year interfere with denitrification and result in decreased N loss through denitrification. The conversion of NO\(_3^-\) to the more biologically preferred form of N, NH\(_4^+\) via DNRA, means that NO\(_3^-\) reduction has considerable nourishing potential and likely will affect both ecosystem function and services. These results indicate that NO\(_3^-\) reduction may contribute to, rather than counteract, eutrophication during warm summers in estuaries receiving high N inputs. As estuarine sediments provide a key ecosystem function of N removal, excess anthropogenic N input jeopardizes their ability to effectively remove reactive N in Little Lagoon and likely in other impacted ecosystems.

Keywords  Nitrogen cycling · DNRA · Denitrification · Anammox · Sediment oxygen demand

Introduction

In the environment, nitrogen (N) is highly mobile (Delwiche 1970), and a single atom of fixed N cascades through the land, air, and water systems before it returns to the atmosphere as N\(_2\) gas (Galloway et al. 2003). Bioavailable N in the biosphere is increasing from anthropogenic activities (Galloway et al. 2004) and as

</page>

<page number="1">

saturation of the landscape is approached, more fixed N is likely to be transported to the coastal zone (Schlesinger et al. 2006). Coastal aquatic ecosystems are disproportionally important relative to their area for processing anthropogenic inputs of N (Galloway et al. 2003) but are being rapidly lost (Turner 1990) as coastal areas continue to be developed for human use. Coupled with the loss of aquatic ecosystems is the reduced potential of these systems to effectively assimilate, retain, and denitrify N, allowing nutrient over-enrichment of the coastal zone (Valiela and Bowen 2002).

Higher nitrate (NO\(_3^-\)) concentrations result from increases in land use intensity (Howarth et al. 2002), which leads to decreased NO\(_3^-\) removal efficiency and an increase in downstream export to receiving water bodies (Mulholland et al. 2008). Decreased NO\(_3^-\) removal efficiency also threatens drinking water supplies as N contaminates groundwater sources (Burow et al. 2010). Additionally, as climate changes, additional N export to downstream ecosystems may occur as agricultural fertilizer applications are affected by drought, heat, and altered rainfall (Robertson et al. 2013). Currently, many freshwaters and coastal zones in the United States are impacted by N pollution (Baron et al. 2013) and some experience harmful algae blooms (HABs), hypoxia, and increased emissions of radiative forcing greenhouse gases like nitrous oxide (N\(_2\)O) (Codispoti 2010; McCarthy et al. 2008; Rabalais et al. 2002).

Microbial N transformations involving NO\(_3^-\), nitrite (NO\(_2^-\)), ammonium (NH\(_4^+\)), dinitrogen (N\(_2\)), or organic N, can influence estuarine production. Two major pathways of dissimilatory NO\(_3^-\) reduction can determine the degree of N retention in estuaries (Sørensen 1978). Denitrification, by which nitrogen oxides (NO\(_3^-\) and NO\(_2^-\)) are reduced to dinitrogen gases (N\(_2\)O and N\(_2\)), is a reduction pathway that removes fixed N from a system, and, since the final product is less available for biological production than NH\(_4^+\) or NO\(_3^-\) (Howarth et al. 1988), it counteracts anthropogenic N input to coastal waters. Anammox is an additional N sink pathway and is thought to be widely distributed in estuarine and coastal sediments (Nicholls and Trimmer 2009). Anammox oxidizes NH\(_4^+\) with NO\(_2^-\) as the electron acceptor and produces N\(_2\) gas, thereby removing biologically available N from the system. Dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA) is another NO\(_3^-\) reduction pathway, but unlike denitrification, N is conserved as bioavailable NH\(_4^+\), which can further support eutrophication in coastal waters (An and Gardner 2002).

The balance of these pathways depends on a number of factors including salinity (Giblin et al. 2010), the ratio of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) to NO\(_3^-\) (Dalsgaard and Thamdrup 2002), temperature (Dong et al. 2011), NO\(_3^-\) concentration and porewater sulfide (HS\(^-\)) concentration (Brunet and Garcia-Gil 1996). Increases in salinity alter DNRA rates and thus affect denitrification rates as these two dissimilatory processes compete for NO\(_3^-\). Some studies have suggested that as salinity increases, sulfate reduction also increases, which may favor DNRA over denitrification (Brunet and Garcia-Gil 1996; An and Gardner 2002). Sulfide can inhibit denitrification both directly (Aelion and Warttinger 2010) and/or indirectly. Sulfide inhibition of nitrifying bacteria slows rates of nitrification (Joye and Hollibaugh 1995) and consequently, as the NO\(_3^-\) supply from nitrification decreases, so do denitrification rates. At nitrate limiting conditions, the DNRA reaction involves 8e\(^-\) per NO\(_3^-\) reduced and yields a free energy of \( \sim 600 \) kJ mol\(^{-1}\) NO\(_3^-\) (Thauer et al. 1977) and poses an energetic advantage over denitrification (\( \Delta G^\circ \) 559 kJ mol\(^{-1}\) NO\(_3^-\)). Increased NO\(_3^-\) concentrations have the potential to enhance all of these N processes so insight into the interaction between N removal capacity through denitrification and increased N retention through DNRA is essential for understanding how estuarine sediments act as buffers for eutrophication of nearshore coastal waters.

In anthropogenically-impacted estuaries, N cycling can be impacted from excess N entering into the system. Like many anthropogenically-impacted estuaries worldwide, Little Lagoon, located in Baldwin County, Alabama, (USA) has high N inputs. The groundwater in Baldwin County is contaminated with up to 2 mM NO\(_3^-\) mainly from agricultural sources (Murgulet and Tick 2008) and discharges (0.6–2.87 m\(^3\) s\(^{-1}\)) primarily near the eastern boundary of the lagoon (Su et al. 2012). Previous studies in this area have shown that groundwater N in the surficial aquifer was extremely high in NO\(_3^-\), indicating SGD in this system is accompanied by significant nutrient inputs (Dowling et al. 2004) that can support HABs. These HABs are comprised mainly of the diatoms *Pseudo-nitzschia* spp., and bloom events correspond to high submarine groundwater discharge (SGD)

</page>

<page number="2">

(Liefer et al. 2013b). Additionally, as Baldwin County is one of the fastest growing counties in Alabama (United States Census Bureau 2011), NO\(_3^-\) contamination in the groundwater will have a long term ecological and economic impact. Increased N supplies, including N input from polluted groundwater and bioavailable N produced by DNRA, can stimulate eutrophication in estuaries (Nixon 1995), lead to loss of valuable seagrass and reef habitats (McGlathery 2001), and affect valuable shell- and fin-fish stocks (Borum and Sand-Jensen 1996). Thus, understanding N removal capacity through denitrification and increased N retention through DNRA in Little Lagoon is applicable to other anthropogenically impacted estuarine systems experiencing high nutrient inputs. Previous work in this system showed seasonal effluxes of NH\(_4^+\) occurred in tandem with high porewater hydrogen sulfide (HS\(^-\)) concentrations during summer months (Bernard et al. 2014) and led to the hypothesis that *DNRA, by producing NH\(_4^+\) as a dissimilatory end product of NO\(_3^-\) reduction, was a significant process retaining bioavailable fixed N in Little Lagoon*.

Methods

Study area

Little Lagoon (Fig. 1) is a shallow coastal lagoon that is tidally connected to the Gulf of Mexico but has no riverine inputs. The water in the lagoon is replenished solely from precipitation and groundwater inputs primarily on the East end (Su et al. 2012). It is approximately 12.6 km long, over 1 km wide at its widest point, has an average water depth of \( \sim 1.5 \) m, a mean water residence time of approximately 10 days (Su et al. 2012), and sandy sediments. Average porosity was \( 0.2 \pm 0.01 \) and average sediment water content was \( 23.8 \% \pm 0.01 \). Because of the rapid development in Baldwin County, a large amount of NO\(_3^-\) enters the Little Lagoon system through SGD (Murgulet and Tick 2008) and NO\(_3^-\) input ranges from 60 to 300 g N m\(^{-2}\) year\(^{-1}\) (Su et al. 2013). In this region there can be rapid changes in the depth to groundwater (Fig. 1 inset) and episodic SGD inputs to the lagoon (Su et al. 2013). Within the lagoon, three sites were selected (East, Mouth, and West, Fig. 1) to represent the gradient that exists across the lagoon from the input of groundwater. Sites were sampled approximately every other month from February 2012 to February 2013.

Abiotic parameters, porewater, and sediment chlorophyll-\( \alpha \) samples

At each site, point measurements of temperature, salinity, pH, and dissolved oxygen (DO) were recorded with a YSI 556 Multiparameter probe. Triplicate sediments samples were collected for porewaters from bare sediments by hand with a modified coring device (2.7 cm ID), sectioned at 10 mm intervals to 60 mm, and extracted in 10 mL of 1 M NaCl prior to centrifugation, filtering and freezing. The filtered (GF/F, 0.7 \( \mu \)m) supernatant was analyzed for DIN (NO\(_2^-\), NO\(_3^-\), NH\(_4^+\)) and phosphate (PO\(_4^{3-}\)), and represents total extractable porewater nutrients. Standard wet chemical techniques modified for the Skalar SAN\(^+\) Autoanalyzer were performed for all nutrient concentration analysis. Water column and sediment chlorophyll \( \alpha \) (chl \( \alpha \)) content were determined fluorometrically after cold extraction in 90 % acetone from filters and in triplicate, respectively.

Denitrification and benthic fluxes from intact sediment cores

At each site triplicate intact sediment cores (270 mm \( \times \) 95 mm ID; 190 mm sediment, 50 mm water column) were collected from bare sediments by hand and setup in a continuous-flow system (Lavrentyev et al. 2000) in a darkened environmental chamber set to the average site temperature within 8 h of collection. The continuous-flow system consisted of a multi-channel proportioning pump that sent 0.7 \( \mu \)m filtered and \( \sim 100 \) \( \mu \)M Na\(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) (99 atom %) enriched site water ("inflow") at a continuous flow rate (1.2 mL min\(^{-1}\)) to the overlying water above the sediment surface. The positive displacement of the overlying water exited the core through an outflow tube ("outflow") and collected in a reservoir. The volume of water overlying each sediment core was exchanged five times during a 24-h incubation period to equilibrate the cores (Eyre et al. 2002). After the initial 24-h incubation period, triplicate inflow and outflow samples were collected at 36 h for dissolved gas and nutrient analysis by allowing the vial to overflow two times the tube volume. Dissolved gas analysis followed the modified Isotope pairing

</page>

<page number="3">

This station has previously been used to investigate the potential role of SGD in driving nutrient and phytoplankton dynamics in Little Lagoon (Liefer et al. 2013a). technique (IPT) (Nielsen 1992; Risgaard-Petersen et al. 2003). In this approach, rates of \(^{29}\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(^{30}\mathrm{N}_2\) production from \(^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) are quantified and used to calculate rates of \(^{14}\mathrm{N}_2\) production (\(p_{14}\)) (Eq. 1, below); when combined with \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) tracer slurry incubations (below), rates of anammox, and the relative contribution of anammox and denitrification to \(p_{14}\) can be determined (Eqs. 2–4, below).

Water samples were collected in 12 mL Exetainers, allowing the vial to overflow two times the tube volume prior to preservation with 250 \( \mu \)L of 50 % (w/v) ZnCl\(_2\) before being capped. Samples were stored under water in the environmental chamber until dissolved gas analysis on a membrane inlet mass spectrometer (MIMS) equipped with a copper reduction column set at 600 \(^\circ\)C to remove oxygen (O\(_2\)) (Eyre et al. 2002; Kana et al. 1998). Benthic nutrient flux samples (12 mL) were filtered (0.7 \( \mu \)m) and immediately frozen until DIN (NO\(_2^-\), NO\(_3^-\), NH\(_4^+\)) and PO\(_4^{3-}\) analyses as described above.

Sediment oxygen demand (SOD) was measured from oxygen concentrations in inflow and outflow water analyzed with a calibrated microelectrode and a Unisense \(^\circ\) multimeter analyzer. Denitrification and benthic flux calculations (\( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)) determined flux into or out of the sediment using the influent and effluent concentrations, flow rate (1.2 ml min\(^{-1}\)), and the surface area of the sediment (0.00708 m\(^{-2}\)). All rates and fluxes pertaining to N species are expressed on a N atom basis. A positive flux indicates release from the sediments to the water column and a negative flux indicates uptake by the sediment. No bioturbation was observed in any of the experimental samples.

Denitrification and anammox from slurry assays

Volumetric rates of denitrification, anammox, and the relative contribution of anammox to gross N\(_2\) production were determined from sediment slurry incubations. Slurry rates for depth-integrated sediments (0–50 mm) were prepared in Exetainers (Thamdrup and Dalsgaard 2002) with artificial seawater (ASW) (70.2 g NaCl, 3.0 g KCl, 49.4 g MgSO\(_4\)·7H\(_2\)O, 5.8 g CaCl\(_2\)·2H\(_2\)O L\(^{-1}\)) constructed at a salinity of 52 and diluted with deionized water to match the salinity of each site. After dilution, homogenized sediment from 0 to 50 mm was added to the ASW and the incubation bottle was sparged with N\(_2\) for an hour and amended with heavy labeled isotope to a final concentration of 100 \( \mu \)M Na\(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) (99 atom %). Sediment slurry was dispensed to 12 mL Exetainers, yielding approximately 1 mL of sediment and 11 mL ASW with no headspace. For each site, 12 vials total were incubated with three vials stopped at four time points 0–36 h. Incubations were stopped by adding 250 \( \mu \)L of ZnCl\(_2\) and resealing the vials without headspace. Denitrification and anammox rates in slurries were calculated according to Eqs. 5 and 6 described below.

Calculations

Excess \(^{29}\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(^{30}\mathrm{N}_2\) concentrations for intact core and slurry incubations were calculated from dissolved \(^{29}\mathrm{N}_2\):\(^{28}\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(^{30}\mathrm{N}_2\):\(^{28}\mathrm{N}_2\) measured using a MIMS (An et al. 2001). Rates of excess \(^{29}\mathrm{N}_2\) (\(p_{29}\)) and \(^{30}\mathrm{N}_2\) (\(p_{30}\)) production were calculated from the flux calculation described above. Rates of ambient \(^{14}\mathrm{N}_2\) production (\(p_{14}\)) in core incubations with \(^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) tracer addition were determined as (Risgaard-Petersen et al. 2003):

\[
p_{14} = 2 \times r_{14} \times [p_{29} + p_{30} \times (1 - r_{14})]
\] (1)

The \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\):\(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) ratio of NO\(_3^-\) undergoing reduction to N\(_2\) (\(r_{14}\)) was determined as follows:

\[
r_{14} = [R_{29} \times (1 - ra) - ra] \times (2 - ra)^{-1}
\] (2)

where R\(_{29}\) was the ratio of p\(_{29}\) to p\(_{30}\) determined for the cores and \(ra\) was the relative contribution of anammox to gross N\(_2\) production determined in vial slurry incubations. Gross denitrification and anammox rates within intact sediment cores with \(^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) tracer addition were calculated as follows:

\[
\text{Denitrification} = p_{14} \times (1 - ra)
\] (3)

\[
\text{Anammox} = p_{14} \times ra
\] (4)

Denitrification stimulated by the added \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\)-NO\(_3^-\) (D\(_{15}\)) was calculated from the classical IPT (Nielsen 1992) and these amended rates are a measure of the denitrification capacity under field conditions when NO\(_3^-\) is not limiting.

Rates of denitrification and anammox in vial slurry incubations with \(^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) amendments were calculated from the equations of Thamdrup and Dalsgaard (2002):

\[
\text{Denitrification} = p_{30} \times F_N^{-2}
\] (5)

</page>

<page number="5">

Anammox = \left( p_{29} \times F_N^{-1} \right) \\
- \left[ \text{denitrification} \times 2 \times (1 - F_N) \right] \tag{6}

where \( F_N \) was the fraction of \( ^{15}\mathrm{N} \) in \( \mathrm{NO}_3^- \). For months when anammox slurry incubations were not performed (August and November 2012), \( p_{14} \) is calculated as \( D_{14} \) from the IPT (Nielsen 1992). Potential denitrification and anammox rates were converted to an areal basis using the wet weight of the sediment in the slurry. All rates and fluxes pertaining to N species in this study were normalized to one atom N.

Potential denitrification and \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixation from slurry assays

The top 50 mm of sediment at each site were collected in duplicate with a large core (95 mm ID) and homogenized. Potential denitrification rates were measured following the acetylene inhibition technique (Sørensen 1978) but may underestimate denitrification supported by coupled nitrification–denitrification, as this method inhibits nitrification. To triplicate serum vials, approximately 20 g of sediments and 0.7 \( \mu \)m filtered site water were added at various treatments (control and N addition of 100 and 500 \( \mu \)M \( \mathrm{KNO}_3^- \)). Samples were sealed with a butyl rubber stopper, capped and flushed with \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) gas for 10 min. After the addition of \( \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_2 \) (10 % v/v) and a 1-h incubation, headspace gas samples were injected into evacuated 12 mL Exetainer vials and \( \mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O} \) production was quantified with a Shimadzu GC-2014 with an electron capture detector (GC-ECD) within 24 h.

Potential \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixation rates were measured as ethylene (\( \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_4 \)) production from acetylene (\( \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_2 \)) reduction (Welsh et al. 1996) in triplicate from slurry assays containing 20 g of homogenized sediment and filtered (0.7 \( \mu \)m) site water. Rates of \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixation by sulfate reducing bacteria (SRB) were determined after the addition of sodium molybdate as a specific inhibitor of the sulfate reduction process (Capone 1993; Hardy et al. 1973). After \( \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_4 \) analysis on a Shimadzu gas chromatograph (GC-2014) with flame ionization detection (GC-FID), production rates of \( \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_4 \) were converted to potential \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixation rates using a \( \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_2\):\( \mathrm{N}_2 \) reduction ratio of 3:1 (Capone 1993).

Oxygen and hydrogen sulfide sediment profiles

An additional sediment core was collected from each site (170 mm \( \times \) 95 mm ID) and \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) and \( \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S} \) (measured as \( \mathrm{HS}^- \)) concentrations were monitored with a Unisense microelectrode system with \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) (Ox-500) and \( \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S} \) (H2S-50) sensors calibrated according to manufacturer’s instructions. Concentrations were recorded at the sediment–water interface and in the sediment at 1 mm intervals to a depth of 10 mm from a single profile.

DNRA

Approximately 1 L of inflow and outflow water was collected from the continuous-flow core incubations for DNRA analysis. Appropriate sample volume was determined after \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) nutrient analysis and expected atom % enrichment. \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N}\mathrm{-NH}_4^+ \) was measured in samples, constructed blanks, and standards that bracketed the \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) concentration of the samples following a modified ammonium diffusion procedure (Holmes et al. 1998) that collects \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) dissolved in water by converting \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) to \( \mathrm{NH}_3 \) under basic conditions and then traps the \( \mathrm{NH}_3 \) on an acidified glass fiber filter. Non diffused standards were prepared according to Stark and Hart (1996) to account for blank corrections. After \( ^{15}\mathrm{N} \) analysis on a Europa Scientific SL-2020 system (Stable Isotope Lab, Utah State University), DNRA was calculated from the production rate of \( ^{15}\mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) (\( p^{15}\mathrm{NH}_4^+ \)) during the incubation according to Christensen et al. (2000):

\[
DNRA_{insitu} = p^{15}\mathrm{NH}_4^+ \times \left( \frac{D_{14}}{D_{15}} \right)
\] (7)

where \( p^{15}\mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) is the production of \( ^{15}\mathrm{N}\mathrm{-NH}_4^+ \) and \( D_{14} \) and \( D_{15} \) are the denitrification rates of \( ^{14}\mathrm{N}\mathrm{-NO}_3^- \) and \( ^{15}\mathrm{N}\mathrm{-NO}_3^- \), respectively. This assumes that DNRA takes place in the same sediment layers as denitrification and that the \( ^{15}\mathrm{N} \) labeling of \( \mathrm{NO}_3^- \) being reduced to \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) equals the \( ^{15}\mathrm{N} \) labeling of \( \mathrm{NO}_3^- \) being reduced to \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) (Christensen et al. 2000).

Statistical analysis

To test the seasonal flux variability between sites in Little Lagoon, two-way ANOVAs with site and date as independent variables were preformed. When data

</page>

<page number="6">

could not be transformed to meet ANOVA assumptions, Wilcoxon/Kruskal–Wallis nonparametric tests were used. When significant differences occurred, Tukey HSD or Steel–Dwass post hoc tests were used to determine significant interactions. A Principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted on all biogeochemical parameters to identify underlying multivariate components that may be influencing N fluxes. Spearman’s rho correlation analysis was used to examine the relationship between the principal components and fluxes. Statistical significance of the data set was determined at \( \alpha = 0.05 \) and error is reported as standard error. All statistical analyses were preformed in SAS JMP 10 (SAS Institute Inc.).

Results

Biogeochemical variables that influence N flux

Temperature and salinity

The average temperature at the three sites in the lagoon was lowest in February 2013 and highest in August 2012 and these seasonal extremes differed by 17 \( ^\circ \)C (Fig. 2a). Average salinity followed an inverse pattern to temperature beginning in August 2012 and was lowest during October when temperature was high and highest during February 2013 when temperature was the lowest (Fig. 2a). Prior to August 2012 there was no discernable pattern between temperature and salinity. Groundwater level was found to be positively correlated with salinity in Little Lagoon, indicating reductions in salinity correspond with SGD events (Liefer et al. 2013a) and the lowest salinity observed during August and October 2012 occurred during periods of increasing groundwater levels (Fig. 1 inset).

Chl-\( \alpha \)

Sediment chl-\( \alpha \) content was higher in the winter than summer (rho = –0.548, p = 0.010) (Fig. 2a) and there was a significant interaction between date and site (p < 0.0001). Over the course of the study, sediment chl-\( \alpha \) content was lowest in August 2012 and highest in February 2013, a pattern similar to that observed for salinity. Water column chl-\( \alpha \) concentration was higher in the warm summer months compared to the remaining study period (Fig. 2a) and displayed an inverse pattern to the sediment chl-\( \alpha \) inventory. The highest lagoon average water column chl-\( \alpha \) concentration occurred in August while the lowest occurred in November 2012, roughly trending with water temperature.

Water column nutrients

Seasonal differences in water column nutrients were observed in the lagoon (p < 0.01 for all). Average water column NO\(_x\) (NO\(_2^-\) + NO\(_3^-\)) was lowest in August 2012 and highest in November 2012 and displayed an inverse pattern to water column temperature. Porewater hydrogen sulfide, ammonium, and oxygen profiles

Sediment HS$^-$ profiles displayed a concentration gradient in the lagoon with higher HS$^-$ at the Mouth and West sites than the East site. HS$^-$ concentration peaked in August 2012 at all three sites (Fig. 3a–c) and exceeded 4000 µM at the Mouth site by 10 mm. HS$^-$ concentration was positively correlated with temperature (rho = 0.438, p = 0.047) and pH (rho = 0.442, p = 0.045). Porewater NH$_4^+$ measurements showed peaks in NH$_4^+$ concentration from 40 to 60 mm during May at the East site, 40–60 mm during October at the Mouth site, and 10 to 60 mm during August at the West site (Fig. 3d–f). The buildup of NH$_4^+$ in the porewaters during August at the West site corresponded to the maximum observed HS$^-$ concentration during this time period (Fig. 3). Oxygen typically disappeared in the first 1–2 mm of sediment (data not shown).

The greatest SOD occurred during May 2012, when water temperatures were high. The highest rates of D$_{15}$ were observed in May 2012 at all three sites and ranged from 13 to 55 µmol N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$ (Tables 1, 2). Average DNRA rates were less than 1 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\) during the winter and spring but increased throughout the summer to a high of 168 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\) in August 2012 (Table 2). DNRA rates in May and August 2012 were significantly higher than rates in the remainder of the study (p < 0.03 for all). Variability was also greatest in August. DNRA rates fell again during the fall months to <20 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\). DNRA flux accounted for 5–80 % of the overall NH\(_4^+\) efflux.

N\(_2\) Fixation

N\(_2\) fixation rates integrated for the upper 0–50 mm of sediment and averaged for each site over the study duration ranged from 1.6 to 2.6 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\) (Table 1). Similar to potential denitrification, higher N\(_2\) fixation rates were found at the West site than the East site (p = 0.021), and the rates at the East and West sites were similar to those at the Mouth (p = 0.904 and p = 0.162, respectively). N\(_2\) fixation rates were variable during the study (p = 0.0003) with rates in February 2012 higher than May 2012 (P = 0.033), August 2012 (p = 0.014), and February of 2013 (p = 0.001). N\(_2\) fixation by SRB differed between sites (p = 0.013) with rates at the Mouth higher than at the East (p = 0.008) while rates at the West were similar to those at the East and Mouth sites (p = 0.150 and p = 0.753, respectively) (Table 1). SRB mediated N\(_2\) fixation ranged from 43 to 68 % of the total N\(_2\) fixation in Little Lagoon.

Discussion

Sediment–water interface nutrient fluxes

Sediment NO\(_x\) uptake the majority of the year (Fig. 4c) may reflect denitrification and/or DNRA fueled by water column NO\(_3^-\) (McCarthy et al. 2007) or microbial uptake (Hou et al. 2012). The greatest NO\(_x\) uptake in the warmer months (with the exception of the Mouth site in August) occurred concurrent with the highest D\(_{15}\), DNRA flux (Table 2), and SOD (Fig. 4a). The few instances when NO\(_x\) flux was positive (Fig. 4c) imply sediment nitrification was occurring at a rate higher than rates of NO\(_3^-\) reduction by DNRA and/or denitrification. Positive NO\(_x\) flux occurred despite the presence of HS\(^-\) in the top 10 mm of the separate cores (Fig. 3a–c), and did not correspond with high SOD flux. Generally, high organic matter remineralization and nitrification rates generate high SOD rates (Dunn et al. 2012), however, the prevalence of sulfides in the sediments (Fig. 3a–c) in Little Lagoon suggest that a large fraction of SOD is driven by the chemical oxygen demand attributed to reoxidation of reduced sulfur originating from sulfate reduction (Howarth 1984). This was especially apparent in the warmer months where high HS\(^-\) concentration corresponded with high SOD. Generally, the lagoon average SOD over the study period was on the lower side of reported literature values for other estuaries (Smyth et al. 2013).

The high sediment NH\(_4^+\) efflux during May and August 2012 (average lagoon maximum: 110 \(\mu\)mol N m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)) (Fig. 4b) potentially indicate high organic matter inputs and rapid remineralization, including DNRA. Episodic HABs in Little Lagoon may be fueled in part by sediment NH\(_4^+\) flux to the water column; especially since the water column DIN pool was relatively low (Fig. 2b), despite small variability in the water table (Fig. 1 inset). A previous study in Little Lagoon concluded that SGD N fluxes were up to 42 times larger than those estimated by benthic exchange but found that SGD and benthic NH\(_4^+\) flux rates were similar (Bernard et al. 2014), indicating the relative importance of the sediment flux to supply NH\(_4^+\) to the water column. Compared to other Gulf of Mexico estuaries, NH\(_4^+\) flux in Little Lagoon is at the low end of reported literature values during the winter and exceeds reported literature values in the summer (Cowan et al. 1996; Gardner and McCarthy 2009; Mortazavi et al. 2000). PO\(_4^{3-}\) flux was generally low in Little Lagoon (Fig. 4d), and the highest flux was observed in the warmer months when reducing conditions in the sediment increased from greater SOD and the resulting lower DO concentrations (DO < 75 % at time of sampling, data not shown) enhanced PO\(_4^{3-}\) release. Low PO\(_4^{3-}\) fluxes are observed frequently in estuarine systems (e.g. Boynton and Kemp 1985) and are generally attributed to sorptive reactions with oxyhydroxides in the oxidized surface sediments (Boynton and Kemp 1985). PO\(_4^{3-}\) fluxes in Little Lagoon are on the lower end of the range reported in other Gulf of Mexico estuaries in Alabama and Texas (Cowan et al. 1996; Gardner and McCarthy 2009). Similar positive relationships between higher temperatures and higher inorganic nutrient fluxes and SOD have been reported in other estuaries as well (Fulweiler et al. 2010; Twilley et al. 1999). The sediment–water interface nutrient fluxes were measured in the dark. In the future, inclusion of light and dark incubations could lead to better-constrained fluxes and better understanding of the impact of oxygen production by the benthic algae and its influence on sediment nitrogen cycling (Ferguson et al. 2007).

DNRA dominates NO\(_3^-\) reduction pathways

DNRA occurred at all three sites in the lagoon and rates overall were greater than the D\(_{15}\) denitrification

</page>

<page number="12">

rates (Tables 1, 2), which lent support to the hypothesis that DNRA was a significant process retaining bioavailable fixed N in Little Lagoon. DNRA is performed by both heterotrophic organisms that use organic carbon as the electron donor (fermentative DNRA) and by chemolithoautotrophic organisms that use NO$_3^-$ to oxidize sulfide or other reduced inorganic substrates (Burgin and Hamilton 2007). While this study did not investigate which group was performing DNRA, Little Lagoon has abundant HS$^-$ that could be used as an oxidation substrate (Fig. 3). HS$^-$ has been shown to interfere with nitrification and limit the NO$_3^-$ supply (Joye and Hollibaugh 1995) for denitrification so DNRA can be the predominant NO$_3^-$ reduction pathway in coastal sediments with anoxic and sulfidic conditions (Brunet and Garcia-Gil 1996; Christensen et al. 2000). This is exemplified in Little Lagoon in the warm summer months when both DNRA and denitrification rates reach their peak, but DNRA is order of magnitudes higher and corresponds with the greatest concentration of HS$^-$ and porewater NH$_4^+$ in the sediments, especially at the East and West sites (Fig. 3a, c, d, and f). In this system, DNRA seasonally accounts for as much as 80 % of the NH$_4^+$ flux.

DNRA rates in Little Lagoon are similar to rates in Florida (11–242 µmol N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$) and Texas (0–79 µmol N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$) estuaries (An and Gardner 2002; Gardner and McCarthy 2009), indicating the potential for regional patterns in the Gulf of Mexico. In many systems denitrification rates are higher than DNRA (Lansdown et al. 2012; McCarthy et al. 2007; Tobias et al. 2001) while in other systems DNRA rates are seasonally greater than or comparable to denitrification (An and Gardner 2002; Gardner and McCarthy 2009; Koop-Jakobsen and Giblin 2010). DNRA has been found to occur in many systems globally from estuaries and bays to unvegetated sediments, salt marshes, and seagrass beds to oxygen minimum zones (An and Gardner 2002; Hou et al. 2012; Lam et al. 2009; Smyth et al. 2013) and in unvegetated coastal sediment, the percent of NO$_3^-$ reduction attributed to DNRA ranges from 0 to 100 % (Giblin et al. 2013). In Little Lagoon, the contribution of DNRA to NO$_3^-$ reduction averages 30–40 % over the study period. However, during May and August, the contribution of DNRA to NO$_3^-$ reduction averages 84 %.

In many coastal systems DNRA displays fairly large seasonal variability and often peaks during the summer. This increase has been attributed to higher temperatures that increase SOD and create more reduced conditions in the sediments (Gardner and McCarthy 2009; Smyth et al. 2013). Higher temperatures may also favor organisms that carry out DNRA over denitrification (Dong et al. 2011; Kelly-Gerreyn et al. 2001). Other studies have reported DNRA to be favored over denitrification when there are large increases in salinity (Gardner et al. 2006; Giblin et al. 2010), but in Little Lagoon the highest rates of DNRA occurred when salinity was below 20 (Fig. 2a) and the water table was relatively high (Fig. 1 inset). The prevalence of DNRA, especially in the summer, in Little Lagoon is likely because of a number of factors including temperature, microbial abundance, HS$^-$ concentration, and NO$_3^-$ availability. Unlike other studies that have found a dominant influential factor on DNRA rates such as salinity or OM (Burgin and Hamilton 2007; Giblin et al. 2010), in Little Lagoon DNRA rates are not governed by a single deterministic factor. Instead, given the closeness of the PCA factors, a suite of variables influence DNRA rates, including temperature, HS$^-$ concentration, and NO$_3^-$ availability.

Ambient denitrification rates (p$_{14}$) in Little Lagoon are on the lower range of values reported in the literature for other Gulf of Mexico estuaries [Florida Bay: 0–350 µmol N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$ (Gardner and McCarthy 2009); Texas estuaries: up to 67 µmol N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$ (An and Gardner 2002; McCarthy et al. 2008)]. However, $^{15}$NO$_3^-$ amendment led to rates of $^{15}$NO$_3^-$ denitrification (D$_{15}$, Table 1) that were similar to rates reported for Apalachicola Bay, where it ranges from 5 to 38 µmol N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$ (Gihring et al. 2010a), but lower than rates reported in other northern Gulf of Mexico estuaries. In Texas estuaries, for example, denitrification is up to 200 µmol N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$ (An and Gardner 2002; Gardner et al. 2006; McCarthy et al. 2008), and at other sites in Georgia and South Carolina (Porubsky et al. 2009) denitrification ranges from <1 to 280 µmol N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$. Increases in net N$_2$ flux after $^{15}$NO$_3^-$ addition indicate that denitrification may be substrate limited, as water column NO$_3^-$ was low (Fig. 2b) compared to other estuarine systems (Boyer et al. 1999; Lehrter 2006; Mortazavi et al. 2000) and was suggested by a previous study in this system (Bernard et al. 2014).

However, denitrification values from the potential assays (Table 1), though not directly comparable to

</page>

<page number="13">

rates from intact cores, show no significant differences between controls and N amended treatments, suggesting another factor such as HS\(^{-}\) inhibition may account for the low in situ denitrification rates. Potential denitrification rates averaged over the course of the study were higher than denitrification rates calculated from \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) amended intact core incubations as well as denitrification rates calculated from the anammox slurries (Table 1). Differences in denitrification rates between cores and slurries are expected because the cores are meant to mimic in situ conditions and the slurries represent potential rates at saturating NO\(_3^-\) concentrations. The anoxic slurries will, however, shut off coupled nitrification–denitrification and, if denitrification relies heavily on nitrification for substrate, then denitrification may be underestimated. In a previous study in Little Lagoon we have shown that denitrification is more reliant on water column NO\(_3^-\) than coupled nitrification–denitrification (Bernard et al. 2014), so it is likely that the slurries have higher denitrification rates than the intact cores because conditions are optimal.

Additionally, N\(_2\) fixation was observed at all three sites in Little Lagoon, which was primarily performed by SRB. These findings support the idea that microbial transformations may be N limited and/or HS\(^{-}\) inhibited in Little Lagoon and account for the higher sediment potential N\(_2\) fixation rates than ambient denitrification rates (Table 1). As DNRA is thought to be the predominant pathway of NO\(_3^-\) removal under high organic matter and sulfidic conditions (Burgin and Hamilton 2007), its predominance in Little Lagoon is not unexpected since chl-\(\alpha\) inventories (as a proxy for organic matter) are relatively high in the sediments (Fig. 2a) compared to reported values in the literature (1–300 mg m\(^{-2}\)) (Cowan et al. 1996; Dunn et al. 2012).

The combination of both organic matter degradation and DNRA appeared to produce enough NH\(_4^+\) for anammox production. However, average anammox rates from sediment cores in Little Lagoon were negligible (Table 1) and potential anammox rates from slurry incubations are at the low end of the range of literature values (0–5 \(\mu\)mol m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)) reported for sub-tropical regions (Gardner and McCarthy 2009; Hou et al. 2012). Anammox occurs in anoxic waters where there are suitable concentrations of NH\(_4^+\) and NO\(_2^-\), derived from the reduction of NO\(_3^-\), and may be more important in ecosystems with limited labile carbon or an excess of N relative to carbon inputs (Burgin and Hamilton 2007), such as land-freshwater interfaces (Zhu et al. 2013). Anammox has been shown to be a significant contribution to N\(_2\) production in deep-sea marine sediments across latitudes (Canion et al. 2013; Gihring et al. 2010b; Lam and Kuypers 2011) but is thought to be of less importance in shallower marine and estuarine waters (Dalsgaard et al. 2005; Dong et al. 2011). The mechanistic determination of why the anammox rates in Little Lagoon are low remains to be determined, but likely because anammox bacteria are in low abundance or high in abundance but low in activity from HS\(^{-}\) inhibition, outcompeted by other microbes (Koeve and Kähler 2010) or concentrations of NO\(_x^-\) may not be sufficient to support anammox.

Denitrification can drive aquatic systems toward N limitation and regulate nutrient supply (Seitzinger 1988). However, DNRA may be favored over denitrification under high carbon loading and increased rates of sulfate reduction, which, if continued over time, will lead to a reduction of N removal via denitrification. Seasonal or episodic enhancement of NH\(_4^+\) regeneration could result in shifts in the nutrient (N or P) limiting primary production (Joye and Hollibaugh 1995) so DNRA also has the ability to influence nutrient supply. The conservation of biologically available N by DNRA has major implications for coastal ecosystems and their response to increases in N loading from terrestrial sources. Estuarine systems have nutrient thresholds, and when the nutrient load exceeds the system capacity for assimilation of nutrient-enhanced production, a decline in water quality occurs. A substantial fraction of the N leaving the land surface is likely to be denitrified in coastal waters (Schlesinger 2009), however many factors contribute to which NO\(_3^-\) reduction pathway predominates in coastal sediments (Brunet and Garcia-Gil 1996; Cornwell et al. 1999; Dalsgaard and Thamdrup 2002; Dong et al. 2009). Key environmental controls that determine whether NO\(_3^-\) will be reduced to N\(_2\) gas or NH\(_4^+\) include microbial generation time, supply of NO\(_2^-\) levels relative to NO\(_3^-\), and the C:N ratio (Kraft et al. 2014). Carbon limitation in the presence of excess NO\(_3^-\) should favor denitrification while elevated HS\(^{-}\) concentrations that decrease the rate of NO\(_2^-\) production relative to the rate of NO\(_3^-\) production would favor DNRA over denitrification (Kraft et al. 2014).

In unvegetated sediment, the DNRA contribution to NO\(_3^-\) reduction ranges from <3 to >60–99 % (Giblin et al. 2013) and can be more prevalent than denitrification. In tropical estuaries DNRA is found to be predominant over denitrification and anammox (Dong et al. 2011) and N loss to the atmosphere is minimized. In environments where high sulfide levels inhibit nitrification or denitrification, a negative feedback between increased N inputs and N removal occurs when DNRA rates are greater than denitrification rates and fixed N is retained in the system, (An and Gardner 2002; Gardner and McCarthy 2009), which potentially exacerbates eutrophication. Together, these results demonstrate that the prominence of DNRA in Little Lagoon has considerable potential to support primary productivity and likely will affect both ecosystem function and services. The N that is retained in the lagoon as NH\(_4^+\) could potentially support primary production (Howarth 1988) and fuel HABs. In the anthropogenically impacted Little Lagoon, the link between episodic HABs (Liefer et al. 2009) and the net amount of DNRA producing NH\(_4^+\) and assimilation by HAB species that augment coastal eutrophication remains to be determined.

A plethora of marine and economic problems stem from nutrient over-enrichment to coastal waters through N contaminated SGD or terrestrial input. These include increased occurrences of marine diseases and outbreaks of HABs (Harvell et al. 1999), increased turbidity and loss of submerged aquatic vegetation, O\(_2\) deficiency, disruption of ecosystem functioning, loss of habitat and an ensuing loss of $2500 per acre per year worth of N removal (Piehler and Smyth 2011), loss of biodiversity, food web shifts, and loss of harvestable fisheries (Rabalais 2002). Coastal eutrophication linked to fisheries decline in the Gulf of Mexico is estimated to cost $56 per kilogram of excess N released (Suddick et al. 2013), signifying the importance of N removal as an economic service. In coastal areas, increased HAB frequency has economic costs to fisheries and tourism (Rabalais 2002). For example, in Alabama coastal waters, toxic blooms of *Pseudo-nitzschia* spp. have been shown to transfer domoic acid, the causative agent of amnesic shellfish poisoning, to recreationally and commercially important fish species (Liefer et al. 2013b), which can cause harm and mortality in birds, marine mammals, and humans (Goldstein et al. 2008; Todd 1993; Wright et al. 1989). These economic and environmental impairment scenarios are likely to continue in the future as perturbations to both climate and the N cycle will cause additive or synergistic multiple stressors to ecosystem function (Suddick et al. 2013) and ultimately affect human health.

Summary

Sediments have an important role in nutrient dynamics by providing sites for denitrification, which, in conjunction with mineralization and other processes such as DNRA, can regulate ecosystem nutrient availability. The most interesting finding of this study is that DNRA is the major NO\(_3^-\) reduction pathway in Little Lagoon, especially in the summer months. Sulfidic sediments in the lagoon during the majority of the year interfere with denitrification and result in decreased N removal. N\(_2\) loss from the system via denitrification and, to a lesser degree, anammox did occur in Little Lagoon, but were orders of magnitude lower than DNRA. These results indicate that the conversion of NO\(_3^-\) to the more biologically preferred form of N, NH\(_4^+\) via DNRA, may contribute to, rather than counteract, eutrophication during warm summers and potentially support primary production and the episodic HABs that occur in this lagoon, though the direct relationships have yet to be determined. As estuarine sediments provide a key ecosystem function of N removal, excess anthropogenic N input via SGD in Little Lagoon may jeopardize their ability to effectively remove reactive N from the biosphere through denitrification and support the DNRA pathway, which will affect both ecosystem function and services in the lagoon. Lastly, as coastal areas continue to be developed for human use, these systems then have a reduced potential to effectively assimilate, retain, and denitrify N, allowing nutrient over-enrichment of the coastal zone and a plethora of ensuing marine and economic problems.

OPEN Associative nitrogen fixation in nodules of the conifer Lepidothamnus fonkii (Podocarpaceae) inhabiting ombrotrophic bogs in southern Patagonia Werner Borken1, Marcus A. Horn2,3, Stefan Geimer4, Nelson A. Bahamonde Aguilar5,7 & Klaus-Holger Knorr6 Biological N2 fixation (BNF) in the rhizosphere of Podocarpaceae is currently attributed to unspecific diazotrophs with negligible impact on N acquisition. Here, we report specific and high associative BNF in dead cells of root nodules of Lepidothamnus fonkii distributed in ombrotrophic peatlands of Patagonia. BNF of nodulated roots, intact plants of L. fonkii and rhizospheric peat was assessed by 15N2 and acetylene reduction. Diazotrophs were identified by electron microscopy, analysis of nitrogenase encoding genes (nifH) and transcripts, and 16S rRNA. Nitrogenase encoding nifH transcripts from root nodules point to Beijerinckiaceae (Rhizobiales), known as free-living diazotrophs. Electron microscopy and 16S rRNA analysis likewise identified active Beijerinckiaceae in outer dead cells of root nodules. NifH transcripts from the rhizosphere peat revealed diverse active diazotrophs including Beijerinckiaceae. Both methods revealed high activity of nitrogenase rates in cut roots of L. fonkii (2.5 μmol N g−1 d.w. d−1 based on 15N2 assay; 2.4 μmol C2H4 g−1 d.w. d−1 based on acetylene reduction assay). The data suggest that (i) nodules recruit diazotrophic Beijerinckiaceae from peat, (ii) dead nodule cells provide an exclusive habitat for Beijerinckiaceae, and (iii) BNF in L. fonkii is one potent pathway to overcome N deficiency in ombrotrophic peatlands of Patagonia. Biological dinitrogen (N2) fixation (BNF) by plant-associated prokaryotes is a widespread and effective process of N acquisition1. However, the capability of plants to host N2 fixing endosymbiotic prokaryotes is restricted to few plant species and bacteria2. Especially in peatlands, the existence of such mutualistic associations is restricted to very few plant species. One example is the shrub Myrica gale (L.) that grows in some peatlands of the Northern hemisphere and fixes considerably amounts of atmospheric N2 in root nodules3. Mutualistic BNF in peatlands of the southern hemisphere is not known, but other strategies of BNF can also occur in peatlands. Conifers of the family Podocarpaceae form nodules and host arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi therein as shown for few species4,5. BNF in root nodules of Podocarpaceae has been postulated in several studies for more than a century6–11. Low N2 fixation activities in root nodules were confirmed for Podocarpus rospigliosii6 and P. macrophyllus10 (Table 1). In contrast, an absence of any N2 fixation was reported for P. totara12. Manuel Bulnes 01890, Punta Arenas, Chile. 6University of Münster, ILÖK, Hydrology group, Heisenbergstr, 2, 48149, Münster, Germany. 7ONG AMA Torres del Paine, Estancia Cerro Paine S/N, Torres del Payne, Chile. Literature data were recalculated to nodulated roots and for dry weight to allow for comparison. *assuming 38% nodule mass per root mass7; †assuming 10% dry matter per fresh weight; ‡assuming a conversion factor of acetylene reduction to nitrogen fixation of 2; §This study, root samples only. N2 fixation activities arise from methodological artifacts and free-living diazotrophs in the rhizosphere, possibly due to incomplete removal of rhizosphere soil11,13. Podocarpaceae are restricted to nutrient poor environments of the Southern Hemisphere14. Many nutrient poor Sphagnum bogs of Patagonia host the podocarp Lepidothamnus fonkii (Phil), a small coniferous shrub of up to 30–60 cm height with hitherto unknown associated N2 fixation (Fig. 1A). Pristine ombrotrophic bogs receive inorganic N from two sources: (i) atmospheric deposition and (ii) N2 fixation by non-symbiotic diazotrophic microorganisms15–19. Atmospheric N deposition is secondary relative to BNF as indicated by exceptionally low atmospheric deposition rates of less than 0.1 g N m−2 yr−120 and BNF associated with Sphagnum or other mosses ranging from 0.5–6.4 g N m−2 yr−121. Net N retention rates and thus N storage in the peat of 2.0 g m−2 yr−1 reported for northern Alberta bogs were mainly attributed to BNF17. Patagonian bogs could have net N retention of 0.4–1.0 g N m−2 yr−1 based on published carbon (C) storage rates of 15–40 g C m−2 yr−1 in Yu et al.22 and average C/N ratios of about 40 in the top 1 m19,23. BNF thus likely represents the predominant N source (0.4–1.2 g N m−2 yr−1) in Patagonian bogs given the low N deposition. The widespread occurrence of L. fonkii in such habitats and the limited knowledge on BNF in Podocarpaceae nodules necessitates studies on the potential of L. fonkii for BNF. Thus, our objectives were to (i) assess associative N2 fixation in root nodules of L. fonkii, (ii) to identify the genetic potential for diazotrophy in root nodules as well as active diazotrophs, and to (iii) estimate the importance of L. fonkii for N acquisition in two pristine Patagonian bogs. Materials and Methods Intact plants of L. fonkii (Fig. 1A) and peat cores of 100 cm2, 20 cm depth, with L. fonkii were sampled at two pristine bogs in Southern Patagonia, Chile, in March 2014: a 2–4 m deep peat deposit at the Seno Skyring (site ‘SKY’, −52.508667°S, 72.127278°W)23 and a 2 m deep peat deposit at the Seno Obstrucción (site ‘OBS’, 52.135907°S, 72.446037°W). Additional peat cores were obtained at each site using a Russian type peat corer (5 cm diameter), in which we determined peat C and N concentrations, C/N ratios, and δ15N signatures of the upper 80 cm (provided in the supporting information; Supplementary Table S1). L. fonkii grew in communities with Astelia pumila (Asteliaceae), Donatia fascicularis (Stylidiaceae), Sphagnum magellanicum (Sphagnaceae), Empetrum rubrum (Ericaceae), Gaultheria pumila (Ericaceae), Drosera uniflora (Droseraceae), Marsippospermum grandiflorum (Juncaceae), and Caltha appendiculata (Ranunculaceae). For estimates of plant biomass (n = 6) additional intact peat blocks were extruded (March 2013 and 2014). All samples were packed in plastic bags and transported to the lab. Leaf biomass, stems, and roots were manually picked, washed, dried, and weighed. BNF was determined using both the 15N2 (98 atom%, Sigma Aldrich, batch No. MBBB0968V, St. Louis, USA) assay and the acetylene (Riessner-Gase, Lichtenfels, Germany) reduction assay (ARA)24. According to Dabundo et al.25 we cannot exclude that 15N2 was contaminated with reactive N gas compounds such as 15NH3 and 15NOx. A mean contamination as reported in Dabundo et al.25 (e.g. 1 mmol 15N mol−1 15N2) would overestimate the N2 fixation rates by about 13%, assuming an uptake of 50% of the total contamination. We assume that moist paper tissues in the jars (see below) trapped a large fraction of potential impurities during the incubation. After washing and removal of peat particles, intact, non-sterilized plants were incubated in 325 ml glass jars. Roots were wrapped in moist paper tissue to prevent desiccation. For 15N2 assays, the jars (800 ml) were closed, evacuated to ~350 mbar and refilled with 15N2 to achieve about 70 atom% 15N2 in the head space (verified by mass spectrometry). In addition, freshly cut roots (0.1–0.2 g d.w.) and peat without live roots (about 0.1 g d.w.) were separately incubated in 22 ml vials with similar 15N2 enrichment in the headspace as for intact plant samples. In parallel batches all samples were incubated with 10 vol. % of acetylene in the headspace for the ARA. To mimic oxygen concentrations in the rhizosphere, we adjusted O2 concentrations to about 2%. Three replicates per site, each with 2–3 intact plants per jar were incubated for 65 hours at 15 °C in a climate chamber with 12 hours light per day (about 500 μmol s−1 photon flux). In the ARA, ethylene (C2H4) concentrations were analyzed after 0, 6, 12 and 24 hours (L. fonkii samples) or after 0, 1.5 and 5 h (T. repens controls), C2H4 production rates were obtained from linear increase of concentration over time and expressed in μmol C2H4 g−1 d.w. d−1. All ethylene time series were highly linear, with an r2 > 0.95. From 15N2 incubations, jars were opened and the plants were separated into roots, stems, and leaf biomass. After oven drying at 40 °C, the dry weight was determined and the material was milled for subsequent isotope analysis. In addition to intact plant incubations, three replicates per site of cut roots of L. fonkii were incubated separately in 20 ml flasks at 15 °C in the dark for 72 hours. As a control, parallel incubations of fresh, nodulated roots of Trifolium repens were carried out in triplicate. N2 fixation in the incubation Figure 1. Moreover, longer incubation times would also overcome at least in part methodological issues of an underestimation of rates due to incomplete equilibration of the added gas (acetylene or \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\)) and the water phase\(^{29}\) surrounding the samples of wetland plants. Concentrations of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) in the headspace were analyzed using a Delta Plus XL isotope ratio mass spectrometer (Thermo Finnigan, Bremen, Germany), after equilibration of the masses 28, 29, and 30 in a microwave (GMW 24–201, AHF Analysentechnik, Tübingen, Germany)\(^{30}\). Ethylene concentration was analyzed by gas chromatography (Model 8610C, SRI Instruments Inc., Las Vegas, NV, USA). Peat and plant analysis for \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) was done using a Eurovector/HEKAtech Elemental CNS analyzer (HEKAtech, Wegberg, Germany) coupled to a Nu Horizon isotope ratio mass spectrometer (Nu Instruments, Wrexham, UK). Sections of *L. fonkii* roots were fixed in glutaraldehyde (2%) and OsO\(_4\) (2%) prior to positive staining with uranylacetate (2%) for ultrastructural analyses. For taking images with scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Philips ESEM XL 30), fixed sections were dehydrated in acetone, followed by critical point drying and sputtering with a gold layer. For transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Zeiss CEM 902 or a JEOL JEM-2110) sections were dehydrated in ethanol/propylenoxid, embedded in epon, and thin sections (50–70\(\mu\)M thickness) were produced in a Leica Ultracut UCT microtome. Nitrogenase encoding genes (*nifH*) and transcripts, as well as 16S rRNA were analyzed from *L. fonkii* roots and peat to identify microbes driving N\(_2\) fixation and those colonizing roots. One mixed, representative sample of young densely nodulated roots from multiple individuals (600 mg) of *L. fonkii* were washed 2x with 70% ethanol and 3x with sterile phosphate buffered saline to remove root surface attached microbes prior to pestling and DNA/RNA extraction with the RNA PowerSoil and DNA Elution Accessory Kit (MoBio, Carlsbad, CA, USA). A representative, mixed sample of peat was extracted in a similar way. Reverse transcription was done with random hexamer priming and SuperScriptIII reverse transcriptase (Invitrogen, Karlsruhe, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s protocol\(^{31}\). *nifH* was PCR amplified from DNA and cDNA of roots and peat with primers IGK3 (GCI WTH TAY GGI AAR GGI GGI ATH GGI AA) and DVV (ATI GCR AAI CCI CCR CAI ACI ACR TC) currently covering the broadest range of *nifH* diversity (including *nifH* of Cyanobacteria) utilizing the Kappa2G Robust HotStart PCR Kit (Peqlab, Nuremberg, Germany) as described\(^{32}\). In brief, reaction mixtures contained 1x buffer A, 0.2 mM of each dNTP, 1.0\(\mu\)M of each primer, 1x KAPPA Enhancer 1, 2.5 mM MgCl\(_2\), and 1 unit of KAPPA2G Robust HotStart DNA polymerase. Thermal protocol was: Initial denaturation at 95\(^\circ\)C (5 min); 40 cycles of 95\(^\circ\)C (1 min), 58\(^\circ\)C (0.5 min), and 72\(^\circ\)C (1 min); final elongation at 72\(^\circ\)C (5 min). PCR products were gel purified, ligated into pGEM-T (PROMEGA, Madison, WI, USA) and TOP10 competent cells were transformed. Four gene libraries were constructed (i.e., one each for root DNA, root cDNA; peat DNA, peat cDNA). Per gene library, plasmids were extracted from 96 clones, and inserts were Sanger sequenced (4 gene libraries x 96) at LGC genomics (Berlin, Germany). *nifH* sequences were clustered with JAGUC2 and OTUs were called at 97% sequence similarity\(^{33,34}\). Cluster representatives were phylogenetically affiliated with BLASTX\(^{35}\). 264 *nifH* genes and transcripts grouping into 2\(\alpha\)TUs were recovered and are presented in the supporting information (Tables S3, S4). Diversity measures were calculated as described in Palmer *et al.*\(^{34}\). Coverages for all gene libraries were always >85%. 16S rRNA amplicons originating from RNA, were generated from roots and peat with primers 341F-785R as described\(^{36}\). Sequencing of the two amplicon libraries was done on the Illumina MiSeq V3 platform at LGC Genomics (Berlin, Germany) and approximately 13,000 quality-filtered reads were obtained per amplicon library. 16S rRNA derived sequences were analyzed with the QIIME pipeline\(^{37}\). In particular, OTUs were called at 97% sequence similarity and OTU representatives were aligned using PyNast. Chimeras were excluded using ChimeraSlayer, and taxonomy was assigned to OTU representatives using RDP classifier. Results Root, stem and leaf biomass of *L. fonkii* (\(n = 6\)) studied in Patagonia at both sites SKY and OBS amounted to means of 221 (range 79–367), 135 (range 49–225) and 119 (range 10–255) g d.w. m\(^{-2}\), respectively. Roots of *L. fonkii* had diameters of <1 mm and were densely covered by 15–20 nodules cm\(^{-1}\) (Fig. 1B,C). After incubation of *L. fonkii* from both sites with \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\), fixed \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) was recovered in nodulated roots, stems, and leaf biomass, resulting in \(^{8^{15}}\mathrm{N}\) values of 4470 \(\pm\) 1730, 3340 \(\pm\) 1270, and 905 \(\pm\) 245\%, respectively. Estimated BNF from \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) uptake into roots of intact plants were higher compared to rates obtained from incubation of cut roots (Table 2). Latter yielded about 70% of BNF in nodulated roots of control white clover plants (*Trifolium repens*) (Table 2). Ethylene production rates in cut roots of *L. fonkii* were about 8 times lower than ethylene production [i.e. acetylene reduction assay (ARA) as a proxy for nitrogenase activity] of *T. repens* cut roots. On the other hand, ethylene production rates of intact *L. fonkii* plants were similar to rates of cut roots. Both N\(_2\) fixation and ethylene production rates were lowest for root-free peat from 20 cm depth. Scanning and transmission electron microscopy of roots or root thin sections indicated a high abundance of encapsulated, gram-negative bacteria with lipoid bodies and intact outer and inner membranes in presumably dead, peripheral cells of the nodules (Fig. 1C–F) of *L. fonkii* roots. Capsules and encapsulated cells resembled morphologies of *Beijerinckia* sp. grown in nitrogen free medium\(^{38}\). Nitrogenase encoding *nifH* genes and transcripts were diverse in peat and included operational taxonomic units (OTUs) related to *Rhizobiales*, *Burkholderiales*, and *Desulfarculales* (Fig. 2, Supplementary Tables S3, S4). Gene and transcript libraries of roots rather than those of peat were predominated by OTU3 that is closely related to *nifH* from *Beijerinckiaceae* (Supplementary Tables S3, S4). The relative abundance of OTU3 transcripts in root libraries was >93%, which indicates active N\(_2\) fixation by essentially one dominating group of root nodule-associated microbes. 16S rRNA analysis likewise revealed *Beijerinckiaceae* associated with roots rather than peat (Supplementary Figure S1).

Discussion Our finding of BNF, indicated by both 15N2 uptake and ARA, refute the common view that the BNF activity of Podocarpaceae is related to unspecific diazotrophs in the rhizosphere11,13. Although there is no endophytic symbiosis, electron microscopy and nifH transcripts indicated abundant living gram-negative bacteria in peripheral dead cells of root nodules of L. fonkii. Interestingly, nodulated roots of L. fonkii displayed similar rates of BNF as roots of a model plant with typical symbiotic N2 fixation by diazotrophic Rhizobia in nodules (Table 2; ref. 39). N2 fixation and ethylene production rates of other Podocarpaceae species, such as P. lawrencei7 were substantially lower than, but for P. rospigliosii6 of similar magnitude as those of L. fonkii roots when calculated on an entire root basis (Table 1). C2H4/15N2 ratios of 1.9–4.9 for L. fonkii fell in a range typically observed for most important nitrogenases40. We cannot exclude that a contamination of the applied 15N2 gas with 15NH3 or 15NOx resulted in an overestimation of the BNF rate25. This bias, however, is likely small in our case, considering comparably high 15N enrichment, the acetylene reduction rates and respective C2H4/15N2 ratios observed for nodulated roots of T. repens, which compared well to values reported for T. pratense41. A significant contamination of the applied 15N2 gas and absorption of 15NH3 or 15NOx could have led to lower C2H4/15N2 ratios and to an overestimation of N2 fixation rates of about 13%. Nitrogenase genes (nifH) affiliating with Bradyrhizobiaceae and Burkholderiaceae were associated with peat and to some extent in L. fonkii roots (Fig. 2). Such diazotrophs were also detected in other studies on root-associated BNF of trees, but the diversity of active diazotrophs was much higher in these studies, indicating a non-specific association of diazotrophs with tree roots42,43. In our study, however, the expression of Bradyrhizobiaceae and Burkholderiaceae related nifH was essentially only detected in peat, indicating that free-living Bradyrhizobiaceae and Burkholderiaceae contribute to BNF in peat rather than to BNF in root nodules of L. fonkii. Accordingly, we assume that these taxa make a substantial contribution to BNF in the peat at our study sites. As Bradyrhizobiaceae and Burkholderiaceae are abundant taxa in peatlands or in other acidic and organic matter rich soils44,45,39, they could be key organisms for BNF in N limited ecosystems (see discussion below). Despite the relatively small importance for BNF in root nodules of L. fonkii, active Bradyrhizobiaceae colonized roots of L. fonkii rather than peat as indicated by 16 rRNA amplicon sequencing (Fig. S1). Rhizobial Nod factors were reported to suppress plant innate immune response in nonlegumes46. Thus, it is tempting to speculate that initial colonization of roots by Bradyrhizobiaceae might enable subsequent colonization of other microbes. The predominant and active N2 fixing, gram-negative bacteria of the Beijerinckiaceae identified in root nodules of L. fonkii (Figs 1 and 2) are well known as free-living diazotrophic bacteria that occur in water and soil including the rhizosphere of acidic peat soils38,47. Beijerinckiaceae-like nifH genes were recently also detected in association with Sphagnum mosses in an alpine bog48. Microbial diazotrophy accounted for most of the new N input associated with Sphagnum mosses17. Thus, plant associated diazotrophy was until recently underrated in bogs and in particular the role of diazotrophic Beijerinckiaceae may merit further attention. Our study provides evidence that L. fonkii root associated, active diazotrophs fix substantial amounts of atmospheric N2. 15N2 enrichment in stems and leaf biomass supports significant and rapid translocation of fixed N excreted or leaking from diazotrophs in the root nodules to aboveground tissues (Table 2). Our results strongly support that this occurs in a specific association with Beijerinckiaceae in nodulated roots and refutes that reported N2 fixation by Podocarpaceae may only result from the activity of free-living bacteria in the rhizosphere13. Observed ranges of natural abundance of 15N in other Podocarpaceae, e.g. δ15N of −8 to −3‰ for P. hallii and P. urbanii49,50, suggest that such associated nitrogen fixation is certainly not a general feature of Podocarpaceae, however, or at least its contribution may not always be significant. For L. fonkii, specifically the following findings support an effective and specific association: (i) high N2 fixation rates, confirmed by both 15N2 uptake and active acetylene reduction (ii) molecular evidence of nitrogenase gene expression predominated by Beijerinckiaceae compared to a diverse diazotroph community in the surrounding rhizospheric peat soil (Fig. 2), and (iii) electron-microscopic images showing encapsulated bacteria with Beijerinckiaceae-like morphology densely colonizing the peripheral dead cell tissue of nodules (Fig. 1). Intact outer and inner cell membranes and lipoid bodies possibly consisting of poly-β-hydroxybutyrate (PHB) are typical for the gram-negative Beijerinckiaceae, further consolidating the conclusion that active Beijerinckiaceae reside inside nodules51. Obviously, peripheral dead cells of root nodules represent a favorable habitat that allows specific colonization and growth by Beijerinckiaceae. The high energy demand for N2 fixation and nutrients for growth may arise from enzymatic decay of plant cell compounds and dead bacterial cells. The layered ultrastructure of L. fonkii nodules (Fig. 1) suggests that Beijerinckiaceae are supported by continuous segregation of plant cells. High nitrogenase and BNF activities are in agreement with the formation of capsules (Fig. 1) that protects the oxygen sensitive nitrogenase38,52. The widespread occurrence of Beijerinckiaceae in a wide range of soils including those of low pH and high C-to-N ratio, their occurrence in the rhizoplane, and their well-recognized role as plant growth promoting bacteria might suggest a broad relevance for N-input of N-limited systems53,54. Thus, the proposed mechanism of plant-microbe interaction via necrosis of root cells and N-transfer from living bacteria to the host might represent an early variant of symbiotic diazotrophy and deserves more attention in future studies. Indeed, evidence from growth experiments with the model diazotroph Azotobacter vinelandii suggests that ammonia could be excreted by or leak out of actively nitrogen fixing cells and can thus be easily transferred to the plant55. In this latter study, A. vinelandii accumulated up to 50 μM of ammonium and was capable of supporting algal growth in N-free medium. Although 15N recovered in leaf biomass might partly arise from a contribution of foliar endophytic nitrogen fixation, as reported for Pinus flexilis56, a translocation of N from nodules to leaves seems more likely due to higher 15N enrichment in the stem compared to leaf biomass. A dense root biomass further indicates that L. fonkii can play a prominent role in the N cycle of south Patagonian bogs. Keeping in mind the limitation of our laboratory approach and inherent uncertainties in an extrapolation to field conditions, the potential N2 fixation is 13 mg N m−2 d−1 for the two study sites based on live root biomass, stems, leaves, and an incubation temperature of 15°C. We cannot exclude overall smaller and seasonal different N2 fixation rates under in-situ conditions. Greater photosynthetically active radiation may improve the growth of root nodules and thus provides more niches for diazotrophs during the growing season. Lower in-situ temperatures would particularly limit the activity of diazotrophs in the early growing season. Further, we cannot exclude that preparation of L. fonkii altered the efficiency of N2 fixation during the incubation. Despite the methodological limitations, it seems that N2 fixation in root nodules of L. fonkii is one potent strategy of N acquisition in Patagonian bogs. Considering recent studies on N2 fixation, plants and diazotrophs evolved different strategies to overcome N deficiency in ombrotrophic peatlands. Other pathways of N2 fixation include cyanobacteria, free-living diazotrophs or bryophyte-associated diazotrophs17,19,28,48,57, highlighting the diversity and niches of diazotrophs in ombrotrophic bogs. Further pathways of N acquisition, e.g. insect prey of Drosera sp.58, have also not yet been fully evaluated. Comparing the BNF rates in other microhabitats, it seems that L. fonkii root nodules specifically colonized by diazotrophic Beijerinckiaceae represent ‘hot spots’ of BNF and thus of N acquisition. Existence of such specific associations and other reported strategies of N fixation challenge the current view on BNF in peatlands and in Podocarpaceae. References 1. Cleveland, C. C. et al. Discussion Our finding of BNF, indicated by both 15N2 uptake and ARA, refute the common view that the BNF activity of Podocarpaceae is related to unspecific diazotrophs in the rhizosphere11,13. Although there is no endophytic symbiosis, electron microscopy and nifH transcripts indicated abundant living gram-negative bacteria in peripheral dead cells of root nodules of L. fonkii. Interestingly, nodulated roots of L. fonkii displayed similar rates of BNF as roots of a model plant with typical symbiotic N2 fixation by diazotrophic Rhizobia in nodules (Table 2; ref. 39). N2 fixation and ethylene production rates of other Podocarpaceae species, such as P. lawrencei7 were substantially lower than, but for P. rospigliosii6 of similar magnitude as those of L. fonkii roots when calculated on an entire root basis (Table 1). C2H4/15N2 ratios of 1.9–4.9 for L. fonkii fell in a range typically observed for most important nitrogenases40. We cannot exclude that a contamination of the applied 15N2 gas with 15NH3 or 15NOx resulted in an overestimation of the BNF rate25. This bias, however, is likely small in our case, considering comparably high 15N enrichment, the acetylene reduction rates and respective C2H4/15N2 ratios observed for nodulated roots of T. repens, which compared well to values reported for T. pratense41. A significant contamination of the applied 15N2 gas and absorption of 15NH3 or 15NOx could have led to lower C2H4/15N2 ratios and to an overestimation of N2 fixation rates of about 13%. Nitrogenase genes (nifH) affiliating with Bradyrhizobiaceae and Burkholderiaceae were associated with peat and to some extent in L. fonkii roots (Fig. 2). Such diazotrophs were also detected in other studies on root-associated BNF of trees, but the diversity of active diazotrophs was much higher in these studies, indicating a non-specific association of diazotrophs with tree roots42,43. In our study, however, the expression of Bradyrhizobiaceae and Burkholderiaceae related nifH was essentially only detected in peat, indicating that free-living Bradyrhizobiaceae and Burkholderiaceae contribute to BNF in peat rather than to BNF in root nodules of L. fonkii. Accordingly, we assume that these taxa make a substantial contribution to BNF in the peat at our study sites. As Bradyrhizobiaceae and Burkholderiaceae are abundant taxa in peatlands or in other acidic and organic matter rich soils44,45,39, they could be key organisms for BNF in N limited ecosystems (see discussion below).
