Obviously, core incubations are crude, and any short-term incubation is likely to miss any oxidation/reduction processes involving iron and manganese or precipitation/dissolution reactions involving carbonate minerals. Nevertheless, plots of Ca:Cl, Mg:Cl, and Sr:Cl ratios in the pore water relative to that measured in the overlying water suggest supersaturation, and thus some precipitation of carbonate minerals. This idea is supported by the calculated patterns of the saturation states of calcite and aragonite at most of the sites (Fig. 4). The mixed terrigenous–carbonate sediments on this shelf are Fe-poor (\( \leq 200 \) ppm) and iron sulfide precipitation is likely limited compared to river-dominated shelf environments, leading to dissolution due to production of carbonic acid by (mostly) aerobic respiration in surface deposits. The rates of DIC generated in the subsurface sediment incubations are not in balance with the amounts of Ca, Mg, and Sr calculated to precipitate in the deeper sediments, but the relationship between sulfate reduction and carbonate mineral kinetics is complex and non-linear, with aragonite supersaturation occurring at both low and high rates of sulfate reduction (Walter and Burton, 1990), and such may be the case in the GBR deposits. The rates of sulfate reduction were similar to those measured in other regions of the GBR shelf (Alongi, 1992; Alongi et al., 2006), and accounted for 6–62% of total carbon mineralization. Most radiolabel was shunted into the CRS fraction and although sulfate reduction was measurable to 1 m at some locations, most activity was confined to surficial sediments. The diminished role of sulfate reduction at some locations is consistent with low S content of sediment and C:S ratios (range: 2.7–5.5) generally higher than in normal marine shelf sediments (Canfield et al., 2005). Although not as dramatic, this pattern is similar to that found in tropical deltaic sediments off the Amazon and Fly Rivers (Aller et al., 1996, 2004). In this study, C:S ratios correlated with rates of sulfate reduction, and the lack of sulfides detected in the pore water suggests that there is comparatively little preservation of S (or Fe) as stable sulfide minerals. Total carbon oxidation rates did not correlate with sedimentation rate. The lack of a significant correlation suggests that other factors such as mixing/physical disturbance and the narrow seasonal range of water temperature play an important role in influencing rates of total carbon oxidation. Empirical and modelling studies have shown that re-suspension of surface sediments stimulates mineralization by aerating sediments, mixing labile organic matter, and by stimulating bacterial growth and minimizing preservation of carbon (Wainwright and Hopkinson, 1997; Aller and Aller, 2004). In a shallow water column, a tight coupling is likely between benthic and pelagic mineralization and nutrient turnover (Alongi and McKinnon, 2005). This scenario is similar to that suggested by Aller (1998, 2004) for mobile shelf muds which appear to act as suboxic, fluidized bed reactors. Comparison of benthic carbon oxidation with pelagic primary production (M. Furnas, pers. comm.) indicates that the relative proportion of water-column organic carbon production remineralized in GBR sediments is in the range of 30–50% which is slightly higher than the range found in other shelf environments (Gattuso et al., 1998). Benthic microalgal production also contributes to benthic remineralization, as seagrass beds were found, but primary production was not measured, at several stations. Terrestrial C input also contributes to benthic carbon oxidation. Using floating sediment traps, Furnas (per. comm.) measured rates of organic carbon sedimentation greater than 3 × benthic mineralization rates. Most of this material was re-suspended sediment, but nearly a third was flocculent or colloidal aggregates, perhaps formed as a result of microbial mediation and exudation of extracellular by-products, as described by Fabricius et al. (2003) in the GBR. Rapid rates of plankton activity within a persistent coastal boundary layer, coupled with warm temperatures, and intermittent mixing and re-suspension, may foster the production of such material. In subtropical and tropical waters, bacteria, protozoa, microflagellates, and appendicularians are known to exude mucopolysaccharides that may promote colloidal formation (Hansen et al., 1996). The overall ratio of O_2:CO_2 fluxes was 1.3, based on the slope of the regression of the two solutes (Fig. 5). This value is very close to the Redfield ratio, implying that reoxidation of reduced solutes approximated their production, supporting the lack of burial of a significant proportion of the reduced metabolites. There was likely some production of benthic microalgal and seagrass carbon at these locations, given the high water clarity and shallow depths, but respiration quotients are sometimes > 1; for instance, use of model Redfield ratio organic matter C_{106}H_{260}O_{106}N_{16}P_{1} and average marine plankton C_{106}H_{177}O_{37}N_{17}S_{0.4}P_{1} yields respiration coefficients for complete oxidation of 1.3 and 1.45, respectively (Middelburg et al., 2005). 4.2. Nitrogen dynamics The ratio of \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 : \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) production in these sediments (Table 7) is somewhat greater than the C:N ratio of particulate material found in the sediment traps. Furnas (per. comm.) measured an average C:N ratio of 8:1 in Princess Charlotte Bay, 7:1 in waters near Sta. HIG, FIZ, and RUS, and 5:1 off Cairns. These differences between benthic and pelagic C:N ratios likely reflect the differences in the composition of the organic material and the types of bacterial assemblages in the traps and in the sediments. Given the number of different methods used and process measurements taken, our data are reasonable to the extent that the sediment C and N budgets are in overall balance. Like carbon burial, nitrogen burial may be overestimated, although any buried N is likely to be refractory material such as fulvic and humic complexes. Rates of nitrogen fixation were patchy but, on average, a small contribution to total N input as in other marine sediments (Canfield et al., 2005). Our rates were within the range of those measured in reef sediments, including those of the GBR (Capone et al., 1992; Charpy-Roubaud et al., 2001; Kayanne et al., 2005; Alongi et al., 2006). The patchiness of nitrogen-fixing activity corresponds to the patchiness of algal mats on the GBR lagoon floor (Alongi and McKinnon, 2005). Rates of net NH_4^+ release, a proxy measure of ammonification, were rapid as were rates of nitrification. The good match between measurements suggests a tight link between nitrogen transformation processes; any discrepancies may be due to unmeasured DON pools and fluxes, and systematic error as a result of our use of small chambers. Most nitrogen transformation activity appears to have taken place in surface sediments at most of the stations with some, but little activity, below the upper 20 cm. Most of the measurements of NO_2^- + NO_3^- flux across the sediment–water interface indicate sediment uptake rather than release. The mineralization and transformation of N appears to have been rapid enough to support the measured rates of denitrification. Sediment pH was near optimal for nitrification as most nitrifying bacteria such as Nitrosomonas grow best at near neutral pH (Canfield et al., 2005). Free sulfide, which can completely inactivate nitrifiers, was absent. Further, water temperatures were within the temperature optimum for typical mesophilic nitrifiers. The denitrification rates were high to the extent that, on average, nearly half of the input of N to the sediment was denitrified (Table 8). These percentages are at the high end of the range of values estimated from unpolluted temperate shelves and estuaries (Seitzinger, 1988; Canfield et al., 2005), but similar to that estimated by Aller et al. (1996) for off the Amazon. Based on sediment incubations and pore water distributions, Aller et al. (1996) suggested the potential for Amazon shelf sediments to denitrify \( \approx 100\% \) of remineralized NH_4^+, while shelf-scale models and budgets indicate that > 50% of recycled inorganic N from the seabed is lost to the atmosphere. Alongi (1990) earlier hypothesized that tropical shelves may be especially important sites of denitrification in a global context because of shelf-edge upwelling, enhanced monsoonal runoff from land, and the suboxic nature of sediment deposits. Such appears to be the case also for the GBR shelf. Denitrification may be enhanced by the lack of sulfides and mineral sulfide formation in these sediments, as denitrifying bacteria are inhibited by sulfides and sulfate-reducing activity. Other factors that drive denitrification, such as temperature, bioturbation, and the supply of organic matter, were within optimal limits, based on laboratory studies of denitrification and the growth of denitrifying bacteria (cf. Canfield et al., 2005). Few comparative data are available for mineralization and burial efficiencies, especially for nitrogen in marine sediments. What data are available indicate that <10% of N is typically buried in marine deposits (Canfield et al., 2005). Burial of N in these GBR sediments averaged \( \approx 11\% \), presumably mostly refractory material. These values may be lower, and the N mineralization efficiencies higher, given the likelihood that burial is overestimated, as discussed earlier. N burial in carbonate muds of nearby Arlington and Sudbury Reefs were similar, averaging 10% and 7% of total N input, respectively (Alongi et al., 2006). Using a mass balance approach, Brunskill et al. (2002) estimated that about 1% of river and marine organic carbon was preserved on the central section of the GBR shelf, but that 3% of river and mangrove organic carbon was buried in intertidal and very shallow-water sediments. In any case, the data indicate that the vast bulk of labile nitrogen is mineralized rapidly throughout the GBR. 4.3. Regional differences In the far northern GBR, a decline in organic matter input was observed with distance from the Normanby River, underscoring the importance of river discharge to nutrient dynamics on this section of the shelf. The inverse correlations of water depth (distance from land) with nitrogen mineralization and total carbon and nitrogen input support this observation. In the northern section of the shelf, a similar situation exists with the two stations nearest to river mouths (Stas. CNS and RUS) having the highest rates of C input. Stas. FIZ and HIG presumably are draped by plumes in the wet season from the Russell/Mulgrave Rivers, yet this area is open to the SE trade winds and longshore currents. Wolanski et al. (2005) observed large-scale resuspension in this area, with the reefs fringing High Island accumulating large slugs of this re-suspended sediment during summer storms. Our measured rates of benthic nutrient regeneration and concentrations of pore water N solutes are well within the range of measurements made in 1992–1993 (Lourey et al., 2001) indicating no clear change over the past decade. The patterns of benthic nutrient dynamics on this shelf are undoubtedly affected by other factors, such as the across-shelf changes in sediment and bacterial community composition, grain size, and water circulation. Numerical hydrodynamic models indicate that under favorable wind conditions, numerical tracers introduced at the coast can move rapidly across the shelf to the reef proper (Luick et al., 2007). However, most tracers entering the GBR remain near the coast for most of the year, with residence times for conservative tracer particles ranging from 1 to 12 months, implying that any particles in the coastal water column will be transformed long before reaching the outer shelf, in some cases, recycled many times. Further, Uthicke and McGuire (2007) have found differences in the composition of bacterial communities between coastal and offshore sediments that may suggest differences in the relative importance of the various diagenetic pathways. For instance, the bacterial group representing most iron and manganese genotypes were not found in the offshore sediments and were rarely found in the coastal deposits. Despite differences in precipitation and total river discharge, there are very few differences between the far northern and northern regions in benthic biogeochemistry. Although there were higher percentages of total nitrogen input lost via denitrification in the far northern sector of the shelf than in the northern sector, these differences were not significant (ANOVA; \( P > 0.05 \)). The reasons for this difference are unknown, but may include differences in sediment oxygen penetration and the fact that, on average, sediments in the far northern sector had lower C:N ratios (12.5 vs. 29.5) and more N (0.05 vs. 0.03) than sediments in the northern sector. Not surprisingly, the overall average rates of sedimentation and mineralization, and C and N burial, were greater in the south reflecting higher rainfall and presumably greater rates of river discharge, resulting in a higher average rate of mineralization in the northern section (8883 mmol C m\(^{-2}\) y\(^{-1}\)) than in the far north (7805 mmol C m\(^{-2}\) y\(^{-1}\)). It is not possible to readily ascribe the regional differences to anthropogenic sources, although the catchments in the northern sector are much more heavily cultivated than those in the far north. Data from Low Isles taken in 1928–1929 (Marshall and Orr, 1931) suggest that sediments of the leeward side near where we sampled, were sandier. Whether or not this change toward muddier sediment is due to natural or anthropogenic change is problematical. Using the river export data of N and P from Furnas (2003) and making some conservative assumptions of shelf area over which this material deposits (1.0–1.5 × 10^9 m^2 in each section) terrestrial inputs equate to only a very small fraction (<10%) of nitrogen and phosphorus mineralization to these sediments. Benthic regeneration of NH_4^+ and PO_4^{3-} accounts for only 6–9% of the N requirements and 4–6% of the P requirements, for net phytoplankton production in these two sectors. These proportions are much less than the N (13%) and P (24%) requirements for phytoplankton productivity in the central section of the shelf (Alongi, 1989). Our denitrification rates are several times greater than the estimated N inputs from rivers in the far northern (40 mmol N m^{-2} y^{-1}) and northern (100 mmol N m^{-2} y^{-1}) GBR (Furnas, 2003). These estimates are crude, but suggest that other sources of organic matter are necessary to balance sedimentary C:N:P stoichiometry on the shelf. 5. Conclusions Most of the organic carbon and total nitrogen depositing to the shelf bed in the far northern and northern GBR was mineralized, with carbon and nitrogen burial being proportionally less on this shelf compared with other continental margins. Differences among locations in carbon and nitrogen flow related best to water depth and proximity to rivers, with higher rates of cycling in sediments closer to the coast. Sulfate reduction, on average, accounted for 30% of total carbon oxidation. The modest role of sulfate reduction was consistent with C:S ratios generally higher than that in other marine sediments. Discrepancies between \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) fluxes across the sediment–water interface and sediment incubations suggest that \( \approx 25\% \) of \( \sum \mathrm{CO}_2 \) flux was involved in the precipitation of carbonate minerals, especially in the subsurface deposits. Ammonification and nitrification rates were sufficiently high to support rapid rates of denitrification. Roughly 50% of total nitrogen input to the sediments was denitrified. Rapid rates of denitrification were likely fostered by suboxic and non-sulfidic conditions in these deposits, the low C:N ratio of depositing material, and intense bioturbation/disturbance of the surface sediment fabric. The average rates of sedimentation, mineralization, and burial of C and N were greater in the northern section of the shelf than in the far northern section, presumably due to higher rainfall and river discharge; phytoplankton production was similar between regions. Terrestrially derived material probably accounts only for about one-third or less of the observed mineralization rates, with inputs from other sources, such as neighboring reefs, seagrass beds, mangroves, and shelf-edge upwelling, needed to balance the measured rates of recycling. Approximately 30–50% of plankton primary production was remineralized in the sediments, which is at the high end of the range found on other continental shelves, and reflected in the overall O_2:CO_2 flux ratio of 1.3. Rapid remineralization in these sediments is attributed to the deposition of high-quality organic material, the shallow nature of the shelf, warm year-round temperatures, and episodes of physical disturbance from cyclones and trawling. These factors foster physicochemical conditions favorable for maintaining rapid rates of microbial decomposition. The rapid and highly efficient recycling and retention of nutrients on the inner and middle shelf, often within coastal boundary layers, may help to explain why the outer shelf reefs remain relatively pristine. Obviously, core incubations are crude, and any short-term incubation is likely to miss any oxidation/reduction processes involving iron and manganese or precipitation/dissolution reactions involving carbonate minerals. Nevertheless, plots of Ca:Cl, Mg:Cl, and Sr:Cl ratios in the pore water relative to that measured in the overlying water suggest supersaturation, and thus some precipitation of carbonate minerals. This idea is supported by the calculated patterns of the saturation states of calcite and aragonite at most of the sites (Fig. 4). The mixed terrigenous–carbonate sediments on this shelf are Fe-poor (\( \leq 200 \) ppm) and iron sulfide precipitation is likely limited compared to river-dominated shelf environments, leading to dissolution due to production of carbonic acid by (mostly) aerobic respiration in surface deposits.
